records.text: Strait of Hormuz exposure for Big Oils For our Big Oils coverage, we have looked specifically at Qatar, the UAE and Iraq production exposure, as these volumes sit on (or are commercially reliant on) export routes that could be disrupted in a Strait of Hormuz stress scenario. While assessing the production impact from Hormuz disruption on our coverage, we note that for TotalEnergies and BP , Abu Dhabi onshore volumes have not yet been disrupted since those volumes are being exported via pipeline. For the group: On the upstream side, Shell has Hormuz exposure through Qatar‑linked upstream volumes, via Qatargas 4 and the high-margin Pearl GTL. TotalEnergies has the broadest footprint across Qatar (Qatargas 2 Train 5), the UAE (onshore and offshore) and a smaller Iraq position, although c.30% of those volumes come from associates production. OMV, ENI and BP are exposed via the UAE and Iraq, while Equinor, Galp and Repsol have no meaningful upstream exposure in these geographies. On the downstream side, we also flag ADNOC refining exposure for ENI (20% stake) and OMV (15% stake), and Borouge Plc exposure for OMV (36% stake). As a result, OMV appears the most exposed among Big Oils to the Strait of Hormuz at the EBIT level. Japan's terms of trade deterioration and real yen depreciation: There is a similar background to the recent declines in the yen's real exchange rate to levels lower than even those seen in the early 1970s, which have of course made Japanese goods, services and labour increasingly cheap by international standards. Productivity has been improving, but unless those gains are reflected in wages, the resultant lack of upward pressure on unit labour costs is liable to depress both wages and prices in relative terms, thereby further eroding the yen's real value. While many may blame the yen's sharp depreciation over the past few years on the Bank of Japan’s tardiness in hiking its policy rate, it appears that Japan's continuing currency weakness needs to be attributed to more than just financial factors such as interest rate differentials. A decline in the real exchange rate is not necessarily synonymous with deterioration in the terms of trade, but in the case of Japan, both have often happened simultaneously in what might be considered different expressions of the same economic phenomenon. records.text: Agricultural imports remain a key strategic tool for China Source: Bloomberg, SPGlobal, Citi Research China inventories of corn and soybeans have been growing recently. China's soybean inventories are likely to remain comfortable and could continue to build over the near term, supported by higher imports and still-elevated crush volumes. However, the pace of inventory accumulation may slow in the second half of 2026/27. Forward crush economics have weakened. As a result, China could continue importing large soybean volumes while crushing growth moderates, leading to a gradual build in inventories rather than a sharp increase. From a global balance-sheet perspective, this reduces the risk of an immediate drawdown in Chinese stocks but also suggests that future import demand growth may become more dependent on policy decisions and feed-sector demand. China's grain inventories are likely to continue building modestly, as corn imports remain restrained but are increasingly being offset by higher barley imports and feed usage. records.text: narrowly defined terms of trade also declined sharply from around the mid-1990s into the next decade (Figure 5). The narrowly defined terms of trade were more volatile over that period, as import prices soared due to rises in international commodity prices, but then stopped falling during the 2010s. Another decline was seen in 2022, as the Russia–Ukraine war triggered a surge in commodity prices, but we have since witnessed somewhat of a recovery. Here too it would be misleading to dismiss the deterioration in Japan's narrowly defined terms of trade as merely a reflection of exogenous factors. We say this because a rise in import prices (due to, say, yen depreciation and/or rising international commodity prices) will not cause the terms of trade to worsen if firms are able to hike their export prices sufficiently to offset such cost pressures. Put simply, the price ratio between imported goods and exported goods will hold steady if export prices rise to the same degree as import prices. For instance, Germany and France – which, like Japan, are heavily dependent on imported commodities – have suffered relatively modest deteriorations in their terms of trade (Figure 6). In other words, while a ‘selling cheaply’ strategy might have made Japanese exports more competitive, it was unsuccessful in generating the volume effects needed to prevent net losses from trade (through drainage of income abroad). Weak yen strategy could end up backfiring for economic growth: The limitations of a strategy that relies on currency depreciation to fuel economic growth are evident. Japan's experience has shown that a deterioration in the terms of trade – due to, say, a weakening of the yen and/or a focus on keeping export prices low – can easily impede real income recovery for the economy as a whole. Although some firms might have been content to see their competitiveness improve as lower relative wages and relative prices effectively made Japanese goods and services cheaper to overseas buyers, the nation has failed to see any meaningful improvement in net exports on a real GDP basis, and an increase in losses from trade has moreover proved detrimental to real income. records.text: of global logistics/supply chains. US diesel prices recently rose above 1970s 2 nd oil shock levels, to around their highest levels in the past 55 years. Prices in the US are attracting the attention of the US President and there is increasing evidence that the diesel price shock is starting to impact global activity, with oil consumption restrictions being discussed in the UK, EU and Australia, and imposed in Pakistan in recent days. ■ In terms of the energy price outlook, our base case (we assign a 60% indicative probability) is that flows through the Strait of Hormuz (SoH) normalise by year-end. This could occur via numerous paths (see next slide for details), and our base case reflects the cumulative probability of these outcomes rather than any single pathway. A normalisation of SoH flows would lead to substantially lower energy prices. This geopolitical event triggered a sharp spike in the gamma vol, with upper left jumping 60nvol, reaching levels not seen since ‘Liberation Day’. records.text: Second, we expect the slowdown in shelter inflation to remain an ongoing source of disinflation. Additionally, shelter inflation could be particularly soft in November. Shelter inflation was surprisingly firm in May, reflecting what appeared to be an outlier-driven increase concentrated in the Northeast (Exhibit 6, right panel). Because the shelter sample follows a six-month rotating panel structure, that panel group will be resampled in November, providing an opportunity for the May spike to reverse. Third, the insurance categories that are unique to the CPI are likely to continue declining (Exhibit 7). Auto insurance premiums appear to have more than fully closed the gap with repair and replacement costs, and the CPI component has declined by 5.3% since December. Our model based on regulatory filings suggests modest further declines on net through year-end. The profit margins of health insurance companies—which inform the CPI health insurance component with a lag—have narrowed in recent years, and our model suggests that the upcoming semiannual update to the source data for the CPI component in October could result in even larger monthly declines between October 2026 and March 2027, subtracting 2-3bp from monthly core CPI. Size of the bubble represents the maximum value between price changes in 2015-2016, and 2023-2024 – example of two most recent strong and moderate El Niño’s Agriculture price risks are heavily skewed to the upside over the next 6-12 months, as they face major supply risks resulting from a high fertilizer prices and from likely poor weather related to El Niño (with he only question being how bad the weather impact will be for net global food production). The cost of agriculture production (via higher energy/fertilizer prices), reduce crop yields/output (owing to lower fertilizer and lower crop protection from oil-based fungicides and pesticide availability) and drive up demand for some agricultural commodities (as biofuels to substitute for high-priced fossil fuels). For El Niño-related supply risks, our preferred exposures are palm oil, sugar, and robusta coffee, where weather-related production risks remain highest. records.text: n quantity of imports. So we opted to measure the amount paid for imports in terms of export volume. Our expression for the narrowly defined terms of trade (τ = Px/Pm) implies that the cost of real imports M denominated in export prices is M/τ, which means that net exports on a real income basis – allowing for income flows in either direction due to changes in the terms of trade – can be expressed as NX(GDI) = X−M/τ. A decline in the narrowly defined terms of trade (τ) boosts M/τ, meaning that more will need to be paid for a given level of import volume (real imports) and that real exports will accordingly decline on a real income basis as more income flows overseas. The amount of income that flows into or out of a country due to a change in its terms of trade is termed the gain or loss from trade, respectively, and defined as NX(GDI)−NX(GDP). Gain from trade = NX(GDI)−NX(GDP) = (X−M/τ) – (X−M) = M−M/τ = M (1−1/τ) What this says is that gains from trade will decline – or losses from trade will increase – if the terms of trade deteriorate. This, in turn, implies that even an improvement in the price competitiveness of exports due to higher import prices being absorbed via wage controls and other cost-cutting measures (that is, even yen weakening in real terms and/or a deterioration in the terms of trade) will not boost net exports on a real income basis unless it translates into a sufficiently large increase in export volume (real exports). Six months into the energy shock, the real surprise has been how well growth momentum has held up across DM and EM economies, with the most recent flash PMIs in the US and Europe the latest (arguably overinterpreted) signals of that. In part, this is because the energy complex has proved to be more flexible and diversified on both the demand and the supply side. In part, it reflects the impulse from fiscal spending (for example in the US and Germany) and a broader investment boom spanning AI infrastructure, defence, and energy architecture. In the US, third quarter growth is tracking at ~3% and the unemployment rate has declined meaningfully since the start of the year. But even energy-importing parts of the world like much of Europe and Asia have been remarkably resilient. The upshot is that even though core inflation has been benign so far, cyclical activity has not been an obstacle to pushing rates higher again and is making central banks more cautious about the passthrough of energy prices into broader costs. There are risks to that cyclical resilience if, for instance, diesel prices move higher or a ban on diesel exports from the US add to pressures across other parts of the world that are already hurting from higher natural gas prices. Our answer has three parts. First, the yen entered the BoJ's reaction function when the July statement added foreign exchange to the factors that govern the timing and pace of policy adjustment. Yen weakness is no longer an exogenous input to the inflation outlook; it is a direct reason to bring a hike forward. Second, the intervention of 30-31 July pushed the yen from 162.80 back to the 157s, so the Ministry of Finance put is felt before 160. The ministerial call on Friday was confirmation that the put is still live. Third, intervention and hikes work in opposite directions for JGBs. Intervention strengthens the yen and reduces the need to accelerate, which helps long 2y. Tolerated yen weakness speeds up the cadence and hurts the 2y. What we presented in London is that inside this band the authorities are more likely to act than not, and tolerated weakness is not our base case. records.text: Sugar supply in India could face downside risks Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg Cumulative Monsoon Rainfall (June-August’26) Remains Below Normal Across Key Sugar-Producing Regions Implied India's stocks-to-use (%) ratio is projected to be at the lowest level A strengthening El Niño, below-normal rainfall across Karnataka, Marathwada and parts of Maharashtra, and forecasts for continued dryness through September threaten cane yields in regions accounting for nearly one-third of India’s sugar output. Reservoirs may cushion the impact, but they cannot fully offset prolonged moisture stress during a critical stage of crop development. As a result, we see a growing risk that current production estimates near 30.5mmt ultimately prove too optimistic. At the same time, India is aggressively curbing sugar diversion to ethanol, with sugar-equivalent use expected to fall to roughly 0.8mmt, down sharply from prior years, as policymakers prioritize food sugar supplies. However, the need to simultaneously slash ethanol use and authorize imports highlights the severity of the underlying supply shortfall. Should dryness to continue further, India could face a materially tighter sugar balance than currently anticipated, reinforcing a bullish outlook for global sugar prices and a bearish outlook for Indian sugar production. 187 Prepared for Cayla Buettner

The first wave of the energy shock to inflation looked familiar: headline inflation rose but with little impact on core inflation. The upside surprise came from how well growth held up. The second wave of the energy shock is far more complicated. As we have consistently highlighted, duration matters - inventories, hedges, fixed-price contracts, fiscal support, and margins can absorb a temporary increase in costs only to a certain limit. Supply chains will need to start reacting, and we see this in producer prices. The relevant question is therefore shifting from whether energy and food raise headline inflation—they already have —to whether those shocks persist long enough to slow core disinflation. To help track the transmission of non-core to core, we consider a range of external shocks driving economic crosscurrents: food, energy, and shipping, though the latter two are related. The reality of these shocks, and in particular for energy the downstream spread volatility that impacts diesel, is that we cannot simply take oil or a food price index level to determine the economic effects. The recent diesel price volatility has different and potentially larger implications for core inflation, structurally, than just the oil move we saw earlier in the year. Why, we are often asked, has the US economy proven so resilient to these shocks? While interest rates have risen substantially this year, our financial conditions n index framework implies that the economic impact should be nearly offset by the effects of higher equity prices, narrower credit spreads, and a weaker dollar, resulting in only a 0.1pp net hit to 2026 GDP growth. While the net impact of this year’s market moves on overall GDP is modest, the effects on some parts of the economy—especially the hit to housing—are more meaningful. We estimate that the increase in oil and refined product prices this year, together n with the path our commodities strategists expect through year-end, will subtract 0.3pp from 2026 growth. The drag comes from consumption as higher energy prices erode real purchasing power. records.text: Energy-exposed agricultural commodities face tightening balances Source: GreenPool, USDA, SPGlobal; Bloomberg, Citi Research Palm oil, soybean oil, and sugar exhibit the largest potential stock-to-use tightening under a "Super El Niño + high energy prices" scenario because they are exposed to both supply-side disruptions and biofuel-driven demand growth. We project meaningful tightening in corn, soybean, and sugar balances, as these commodities are uniquely exposed to both sides of the market equation: supply risks and demand expansion from biofuels. Historical energy shock periods demonstrate that elevated gasoline and diesel prices are typically accompanied by higher biofuel demand, as governments increasingly rely on blending mandates and domestic fuel alternatives to reduce energy import dependence and mitigate fuel-price inflation. The effect is particularly pronounced today, with Brazil increasing gasoline blending requirements to E32, Indonesia implementing B50 biodiesel, and renewable fuel demand continuing to expand globally. In addition, ongoing regulatory uncertainty surrounding Small Refinery Exemptions (SREs) in the United States creates further upside risk for soybean oil demand. A stricter approach to granting exemptions would increase Renewable Fuel Standard compliance obligations, potentially boosting biomass-based diesel and renewable diesel consumption and further tightening already constrained soybean oil balances. Compared to crude oil, diesel is a critical product with a much higher/quicker pass - through from prices to core inflation via transportation costs (such as the 8% fuel surcharge imposed by the US Postal Service in late April ; Figures 1 and 2 ). We think diesel export restrictions are becoming increasingly likely as the options available to arrest the rise in oil and product prices ahead of the US midterms are ever more limited. But such restrictions are not imminent, in our view. We consider a release from European strategic petroleum reserves – which currently amount to 189mn barrels of product stocks – as the next most likely and viable step before moving towards an outright export restriction. Other alternatives, such as increasing Chinese product exports or returning Russian and Middle East product output look less likely near term. If none of these levers turn out to be successful in settling down the product prices, export restrictions will become the probable outcome. These restrictions can be in the form of duties, actual volume caps or outright bans, ranked from the least to the most impactful measure (see Running out of options – EU SPR release likely before US diesel export cap , dated 24 September). LLC Global Market Views: More Paths to Relief 28 September 2026 | 3:35PM BST 1. Rates, energy and AI: same risks, better priced. Core rates have pushed to new highs in recent sessions, although so far they have served only to limit the gains in rather than to break risky assets. Similar stories have played out across the three main risk factors we have been flagging over the summer—rates, energy prices and AI. Our baseline views are still mostly benign in each case, but the distribution of market pricing has shifted in a more adverse direction so that the asymmetry is shifting to the constructive side. Energy prices have moved higher, and with diesel product and European gas prices outpacing gains in crude, that has dragged front-end rate pricing up so that we are now pricing 100bp+ hiking cycles in the US, UK and Europe. AI-related equities have recovered somewhat, but the complex has still derated on the back of another stellar earnings season. The risks in each case remain, but with these worries now more clearly embedded in pricing, there are also more paths to relief. Last month we believed that higher yields were the main risk to a constructive view, and that remains true. Compared to crude oil, diesel is a critical product with a much higher/quicker pass - through from prices to core inflation via transportation costs (such as the 8% fuel surcharge imposed by the US Postal Service in late April ; Figures 1 and 2 ). We think diesel export restrictions are becoming increasingly likely as the options available to arrest the rise in oil and product prices ahead of the US midterms are ever more limited. But such restrictions are not imminent, in our view. We consider a release from European strategic petroleum reserves – which currently amount to 189mn barrels of product stocks – as the next most likely and viable step before moving towards an outright export restriction. Other alternatives, such as increasing Chinese product exports or returning Russian and Middle East product output look less likely near term. If none of these levers turn out to be successful in settling down the product prices, export restrictions will become the probable outcome. These restrictions can be in the form of duties, actual volume caps or outright bans, ranked from the least to the most impactful measure (see Running out of options – EU SPR release likely before US diesel export cap , dated 24 September). records.text: Food inflation risks rising as agricultural prices would likely further increase Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg Agricultural commodities are up ~20% year-to-date (BCOM), with significant implications for global food inflation over the coming quarters (please see the chart below). We remain bullish agricultural commodities because the market is facing an unprecedented potential shock to supply, which could result in convex price moves in a number of agricultural commodity markets, and as such the risks are skewed to the upside. The combination of bad weather, lack of crop yield maximization through reduced use of increasing expensive fertilizers, and increased vulnerability to disease (owing to the likely underuse of expensive oil-based pesticides and fungicides), could see extreme supply surprises to the downside, and convex price outcomes to the upside over the coming months. We see the most upside in sugar (+25% vs spot), corn (+17% vs spot), soybeans (+12% vs spot), and wheat (+16% vs spot) across the agricultural commodity complex on a 12-month horizon. records.text: Stacking supply shocks raise agricultural production-at-risk Source: NOAA, Bloomberg, Citi Research Agricultural production at-risk on the back of strong El Niño Agricultural markets are increasingly exposed to a rare combination of weather, input-cost, and logistics shocks. While El Niño remains the primary focus, our expanded Supply-at-Risk framework suggests that prolonged disruptions to energy and fertilizer flows through the Strait of Hormuz, combined with persistent Black Sea export constraints, could amplify supply losses well beyond historical weather- driven episodes. Wheat, corn, and barley emerge as the most vulnerable markets due to their simultaneous exposure to fertilizer shortages, crop-protection constraints, and Black Sea disruptions, while palm oil, sugar, coffee, and cocoa remain highly exposed to El Niño-related production risks. The next cohort, consisting of software loans maturing between T+2 and T+3 years, is trading at $80.51 (Figure 4). There has been a recovery since the lows of the first quarter but many loans in each cohort are trading distressed, weighing on overall sector performance. The dispersion within these cohorts is emblematic of AI-driven disruption. Breaking the T+2 and T+3 cohorts into price buckets, it is clear that market pricing has coalesced around two groups. 1) Firms that should be able to refinance with a normal degree of risk and 2) Firms whose fundamentals appear significantly impaired. Within the T+2 cohort, 22% of software loans trade distressed (below $80), while 40% trade at $95 or higher. The T+3 cohort is even more bimodal, with 42% trading at distressed levels and 48% trading above $95. This pricing suggests that investors view certain issuers as set to be heavily restructured or potentially non-viable, with $13.5 billion of loans maturing by September 2029 marked below $60. It would be the third round after the FY2025 mid-year revision and the FY2026 plan, repeating the template the Ministry set out in the FY2026 plan, cutting super-longs by JPY100bn a month while holding the intermediate sector, this time with the intermediate sector raised. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 Economics | Resilience Now, Some Question Marks Later So far more resilient than expected: The near-term growth discussion was relatively encouraging. Resilience in the face of higher energy prices surprised investors and featured repeatedly in the feedback from Rome. The September quarterly accounts provide some support for that assessment: real GDP rose by 0.2%Q in 2Q26, leaving calendar-adjusted carry-over growth for 2026 at 0.8%. The broad expectation in our discussions was for continued, but moderate, expansion. Limited second round effects from energy so far: One explanation for the resilience is that the energy shock has so far spread less rapidly through the economy than in 2022. The feedback pointed to limited second-round effects and a more contained transmission beyond the energy component of the basket. Going forward, persistence of the shock matters: a prolonged shock could increasingly affect production costs, price-setting and spending decisions. We would therefore be cautious about extrapolating the initial GDP response to the following quarters, in particular as commodity prices remain elevated. The resilience of external demand: External demand was also recognised as a key driving factor behind the resilience. records.text: 3. Hikes everywhere, but more priced. As the energy shock has extended, and product prices have risen further, the major central banks have restarted their tightening cycles. The market is now priced for cumulative tightening cycles (including those delivered in September) of close to 5 hikes for the ECB and Fed and more than 4 for the BOE. That profile is well above our own central forecasts, which are driven by a view that limited core inflationary pressures will limit the depth of the tightening cycle. The asymmetry around pricing is becoming clearer too, with 2-3 hikes much more likely in our view than 7-8. The challenge to receiving rates is that hike pricing remains very correlated with swings in energy prices. Persistent negative correlation between equities and yields also means that we are firmly back in a world where a risk premium in the front end makes sense. We think the Fed is likely to front-load rate hikes with another move in October and meaningful risk of a December move, so paying the very front end of the curve may still make sense. But with deeper forwards (2y1y OIS) now well through the 2023 highs, we think there are opportunities to hedge growth risks further out. records.text: Palm oil supply risks could tighten global vegetable oil balances Source: Bloomberg, Citi Research Lower palm oil production could lead to increased demand for soybean oil, USD/mt Indonesia's aggressive biofuel policy represents an additional source of upside risk for soybean oil and oilseed markets. Indonesia has already accelerated implementation of its B50 biodiesel mandate, increasing the share of palm oil-based biodiesel in diesel fuel to 50%. The higher biodiesel mandate effectively diverts a larger share of domestic palm oil production away from export markets and toward the energy sector, tightening global vegetable oil supplies. Lower palm oil availability could provide an important tailwind for soybean oil demand. Historically, vegetable oil demand tends to shift toward soybean oil when the palm oil premium narrows materially, and the current spread remains above levels that have previously stimulated substitution. If El Niño-related weather impacts tighten palm oil supplies in Indonesia and Malaysia, higher palm oil prices could drive additional soybean oil demand and improve crush economics. Brazil's recent increase in the gasoline ethanol blend to E32 is supportive for corn markets because it raises domestic ethanol demand, reinforces growth in Brazil's corn-based ethanol industry, increases industrial corn consumption, and ultimately reduces the country's exportable surplus. 177 Prepared for Cayla Buettner

The trade breaks even at 5.88%, which is more than three extra hikes from here, covering a total of eight hikes in this cycle. We see the probability of exceeding this level low, based on our economic outlook; 6. Since the trade is short skew, it carries positively about 2.5bp per month; 7. The risk of the trade is a MTM loss of an imminent selloff after initiation. We think the risk is low given yield just sold off 25bp since Wednesday on the back of a confluence macro and technical factors. Diesel and oil products aren’t getting out of the ME, or Russia Source: Energy Aspects, Citi Research ■ As an opening caveat we think it is important to note that the data on global products balances and flows from third parties is giving very mixed signals. The below are rough estimates only and reflect some human judgement using logic and squaring of various datapoints including prices themselves. ■ It appears that the Middle East is exporting around ~4mb less oil products compared to pre-war. This makes sense to us as we are aware that a litany of logistical issues are preventing oil products from making their way out of the ME: – Products are typically shipped on small ships which are more vulnerable to human loss of life if attacked – Products if shipped on a VLCC would be much higher value Iranian target – It would be costly if Persian gulf exporter refineries ramp up and then have to close again – Pipeline diversions are designed for crude oil not products ■ Russia could be exporting around ~1-1.5mb less oil products compared to pre-war – The R/U conflict is resulting in lower refinery output and exports from Russia ■ To the degree crude oil supply from the ME is reduced, Asia refineries have also cut product production and exports ■ Of all products, diesel has been the most affected product market globally, with prices now above 2 nd oil shock levels in today’s dollars. ME diesel exports may be down by around ~0.5-1mb/d, and Russian diesel exports down ~0.3-0.6mb

records.text: Noel Dixon 28 September 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General RBA Preview: Hawkish hold The RBA again faces a difficult choice. Given recent data, will it opt for a hawkish hold or a dovish hike? We think it may surprise markets by choosing the former. Inflation remains a key concern (Figure 1), as higher energy prices are likely to keep headline CPI elevated even as core pressures remain relatively stable. Meanwhile, Australian consumers continue to face cost-of- living pressures, negative real wage growth and a softening labour market, with unemployment at its highest since November 2021. August CPI will be released after the RBA’s 29 September meeting, and we believe policymakers will prefer to wait and assess those figures before committing to another hike. Overall, the three rate increases currently priced by markets look difficult to deliver while consumers remain under strain. Combined with extreme positioning, this reinforces our medium-term bearish AUD view, with short AUDJPY our preferred trade at current levels. Consensus forecasts expect headline CPI inflation to rise to 4.1%yoy in August from 3.5% the previous month, while trimmed mean inflation is forecast to remain unchanged. This aligns with PriceStats, which shows price gains concentrated in essentials such as energy, utilities and food, while inflation is easing across discretionary goods and services. Supply: whichever account funds it, the bonds land in the same market The supply questions came in two parts: how will the consumption tax cut be funded, and will the super-long cuts continue in the FY2027 issuance plan? The first refers to the tax reform outline approved by the Cabinet in September, which lowers the consumption tax on food and beverages from 8% to 1% for two years from April 2027 and defers the funding decision to the year-end budget process. The outline states that the government will not rely on special deficit-financing bonds, but it is far from clear that around JPY5trn a year of tax cuts and payments can be covered by expenditure and revenue reviews, and the prevailing view in London was that "no reliance on deficit-financing bonds" is a label rather than a plan. Our answer is to separate the label from the supply. Whichever account and whichever legal vehicle is used, the bonds sold to the market are absorbed by the same market. The first supplementary budget in May, of just over JPY3trn, was funded without increasing market issuance by offsetting it against bonds that had gone unissued in the previous fiscal year, but that is a device that can be used only once. Our placeholder for FY2027 budget requests is JPY135trn, and if the funding gap falls on JGBs, the Ministry of Finance's tenor of choice is the short to intermediate sector and bills. records.text: US Equity Strategy28 September 2026 ab 7 Valuations pricing higher rates and/or lower growth/margins Valuations have fallen over the last 6-9mo as earnings have surged, profitability has improved and forward growth expectations have been revised up. Markets appear to be pricing slower growth, lower margins and/or higher rates. Given accelerating growth in many areas, the de-rating has been "early" and larger compared to past cycles, but discounting through cycle earnings/margins is a continued challenge. There are many drivers of equity valuations but they can essentially be grouped into: 1) bond yields, 2) cyclical growth, 3) secular/terminal growth, 4) quality/uncertainty, 5) return of capital. Our forward sales growth CAGR is the most significant variable in the SPX valuation framework, on a univariate basis, while CFROI is the most significant variable in the broad P/E framework. The rise in fwd sales CAGR and CFROI has pushed the implied SPX P/E to >24x based on our framework. With ~21% upside to the implied P/E, the residual is at levels seen in 2020 and 2011-12. Our baseline is that valuations remain well supported amid strong EPS growth, with large upside if higher growth does get priced. records.text: Tin – Bullish on structural upside and persisting supply constraints Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg, LME ■ In our base case (60% probability) we see tin prices climbing to $60,000/t in the coming months . We really like tin’s upside potential over the next 6-12 months. The medium-term investment case mirrors copper and aluminium, supported by structural demand from electrification, renewables, and AI, but investor positioning is much cleaner. Supply is less elastic than copper with most major mine sources vulnerable to policy-led or social disruption. The relatively small size in volume and total value of the tin market also make it an easier target for any strategic stockpiling activity and more sensitive to episodes of China retail-led buying. ■ In our bull case (20% probability), tin climbs to average $70k/t, surpassing record highs on scarcity dynamics driven by severe and prolonged supply disruptions among major producers. Given the high concentration of global tin production, supply is structurally vulnerable to disruptions to individual mines or regions. Accelerating structural demand, particularly from solar and electronics, combined with a renewed global cyclical growth recovery, would reinforce upside price momentum and the potential for real physical deficits. ■ In our bear scenario (20% probability), prices retreat to average $45 k/t through 2027. records.text: We have softened our view on the plausibility of a tariff outcome. Any such a move we think would most likely be a reactionary last- resort to keep metal in the country but is hard to call either way. Through 4Q’26 at least we expect the US adminstration to remain strategically ambiguous on copper cathode tariffs and for the status quo to remain largely intact. To the extent that the US adminstration views the market retaining or continuing to build domestic copper inventory as a goal (noting that this is an assumption never claimed by any senior officials publicly) the status quo and fear of a tariff remains more effective than implementation. Therefore, paradoxically, the greater the pricing for a tariff by the market, the less likely we think one becomes in the near-term (and vice-versa) We think the US arb will continue to price some tariff risk until at least the mid-terms. Why Has the US Economy Been So Resilient to Higher Rates and Higher Oil Prices? We now estimate that the economy grew at a 3.4% pace in Q3 and forecast 2.2% growth in 2026 overall on a Q4/Q4 basis, close to our 2.3% estimate of potential GDP growth and only 0.3pp below our start-of-the-year forecast when we did not expect large increases in interest rates and oil prices. In today’s Daily, we ask why the US economy has proven so resilient to these surprises. Part of the answer is that financial conditions have changed little on net since January, as the substantial rise in interest rates has been nearly offset by the effects of higher equity prices, narrower credit spreads, and a weaker dollar (Exhibit 1, left). Our estimated GDP growth impulse from the FCI is therefore little changed from the start of the year (Exhibit 1, right), implying only a 0.1pp hit to 2026 Q4/Q4 GDP growth. While the net impact of this year’s market moves on overall GDP is modest, the effects on some components of GDP are more meaningful. We use the Fed’s macroeconomic model FRB/US to estimate how the particular combination of market moves this year should affect each component of GDP . We find a meaningful hit from higher rates to residential investment, offset by slight boosts to consumption and business investment (Exhibit 2). records.text: US Equity Strategy28 September 2026 ab 3 US Equity Strategy UBS Research After 10y jump, SPX path likely driven by Fed path There are eight events since 1985 where the 10yr has increased by more than 1.5.stddev above the 1yr moving average, including now. Peak z-scores across the completed set range from 1.64 (2016) to 3.14 (2022). The key driver of what happens next is whether the Fed enters a full hiking cycle or adjusts rates moderately in our view. Three of the seven completed episodes began inside a Fed hiking cycle where the Fed rate increased by over 1pp within 1yr of the 10yr breakout (1994, 1999, 2022). The other four did not see larger Fed hikes (2013, 2016, 2021, 2023) . Across all seven completed episodes, the S&P's average forward return from the +1 stdev crossing is roughly flat over the next 3mo (-1.2% at 3 months) before turning higher over 6–12 months (+4.9% 6mo, +10.0% 12mo). In hiking-cycle episodes, equities have historically been down 2.3% after 1 month and down 4.1% after three months. In the other instances, the S&P has been modestly positive over the first month and quarter, then compounding to +10.4% at six months and +17.7% at twelve. There was a ~18pp difference in performance depending on whether the magnitude of Fed rate increases over the next year. records.text: Although the US administration is considering other ways to lower domestic diesel prices, we see some restrictions on diesel exports (including export quotas) as very plausible. Alternatives include temporarily waiving the $0.24/gal federal tax on retail diesel sales and/or exempting road diesel from the federal biofuel-blending program, which would suspend RIN costs worth about $0.30/gal. While diesel export quota/licenses are plausible too and the duration of any export restriction is uncertain, we model a hypothetical US diesel export ban from early October 2026 through at least December 2026 (as a 90-day ban is reportedly being considered). In such a diesel export ban scenario, we believe that US and ex-US diesel prices would decouple while the ban lasts. US diesel production is highly concentrated in the Gulf Coast (PADD3) which is then sent to other US regions (Exhibit 8). Other US regions such as the East Coast (PADD1)—which typically import some diesel from the international market—would likely fully switch to US supply as significant supply from the US Gulf Coast—which has been exporting 1½mb/d of diesel abroad recently—frees up. This switch assumes an extension of the Jones Act waiver, which lets foreign tankers ship diesel given pipeline capacity constraints. Realizing the full switch might take some time as US refiners have already planned some exports and as transportation can take a few weeks. records.text: Iron Ore – Producer breakevens are rising, with cost support above $85/t Source: Citi Research, Company Reports ■ We see industry effective cost support for iron ore producers anchored above $85/t. We recently published the 2026 edition of our proprietary iron ore cost curve, based on a modelled universe that represents ~84% of the seaborne supply. Our cost curve framework suggests at $85/t level, 100Mtpa or 6% of global seaborne supply, would be uneconomical. Based on our analysis, non-mainstream supply (not included in our cost curve) and high-cost producers would be at risk at prices between $85-$95/t. Since publication of our cost curve report, diesel and freight rates have increased further, lifting the effective cost floor for seaborne producers. Taken together, we estimate that at or below $95/t, roughly 100-130Mtpa of supply would be at risk of curtailment. ■ Global Diversified Metals & Mining - Iron ore producer breakevens are rising, with cost support emerging at $85/t Citi’s all in quality adjusted 62% Fe cost curve 157 Prepared for Cayla Buettner

Series is then multiplied by NY ULSD diesel pricing. Rationale is copper price is sensitive to both varying need for marginal tonnage of scrap to meet consumption vs mine output gap and also to the varying cost of scrap recovery (as proxied with diesel price). Higher copper prices are supported by a rising call-on-scrap as consumption outpaces mine supply growth. They are also supported by inflation of marginal scrap recovery costs to meet that gap (e.g. due to higher fuel prices because of the Strait of Hormuz closure and other policy headwinds to scrap supply that in turn inflate cost). records.text: Solar PV silver demand to decline in 2026-27 on thrifting and substitution Source: Citi Research, SMM, NBS, Metals Focus, Silver Institute Solar cell manufacturers have been thrifting and substituting silver to cut costs We expect global solar PV demand to decline by ~22% y/y in 2026, driven primarily by accelerated silver thrifting and weaker solar installations. In 2027, the decline in silver loadings will accelerate as BC solar cells gain market share. TOPCon cell prices have been on a sustained downtrend since 2025, driven by industry oversupply, weak demand growth, and ongoing inventory adjustments across the solar value chain. Silver thrifting has now become one of the key strategies for improving profitability for solar cell manufacturers in China. While silver intensity has already fallen by ~43% and ~68% respectively in TOPCon and HJT technologies since 2023, the producers are now moving towards BC solar cell technology with no silver at all to improve profitability. According to the Silver Institute, zero-busbar architectures and ultra-fine printing could reduce silver loadings by a further 10-20%, pushing silver intensity below 5mg/W by 2027 and reinforcing the structural downtrend in PV-related silver demand. We expect global solar installations to decline by ~5% y/y in 2026, as a sharp ~19% contraction in China more than offsets growth in ex-China markets. In 2027, we expect solar PV demand to decline 15% y/y on BC gaining market share. Global solar installation

records.text: #5: Reiterating Our Long Positions in European Gasoline Hedging Recommendation Fifth, we reiterate our recommendation to hedge geopolitical risk through long 2027 positions in European gasoline (e.g. EBOB Jun27) for three reasons: Gasoline markets are tightening rapidly as high diesel prices have caused global n refiners to switch output from gasoline to diesel. Even higher ex-US diesel prices following potential US diesel export restrictions might intensify the switch of ex-US refiners from gasoline to diesel further. Any future potential inclusion of gasoline in US product export restrictions would n tighten gasoline markets outside the US.7 And even in US diesel export restrictions only scenarios, the eventual loss in US gasoline output if US diesel storage were to hit congestion, would also translate into tighter global gasoline markets once potential US diesel export restrictions are lifted. Europe’s gasoline SPR reserves are about four times smaller than its diesel reserves n (Exhibit 7), which limits European policymakers’ potential to offset further gasoline tightening with SPR releases. 7 High US East Coast gasoline imports from the rest of the world might complicate the full switch to US Gulf Coast imports. records.text: 8 Inflation Strategist | 28 September 2026 The UK faces another fiscal hit from higher-than-expected inflation this year, although nothing like as bad as in the 2022/23 fiscal year (when the interest bill alone rose to more than 4%/GDP). That year, the linker indexation charge plus coupons paid represented almost three quarters of the interest cost to Public Sector Net Borrowing on an accruals basis. For 2026/27, the key print will be the January 2027 RPI, which determines linkers’ index ratios for the 1 April value date marking the start of the new fiscal year. The OBR assumption for this in March was 3.0% and the market’s reading is now 5.5%. By our calculations, this would lift the expected indexation charge from about £20bn to about £37bn (Exhibit 15). As we approach the Autumn Budget, all of this makes us wonder whether the DMO might, like last Autumn, cut the remaining balance of the linker programme for 2026/27 (or at least make only light or no drawdowns from the remaining unallocated portion of the Remit for linkers). Last year, the revised Remit chopped the remaining linker syndication and two of the five linker auctions that were scheduled. Longer term, we wonder whether the linker share might be cut in future fiscal years, if only temporarily. There are the questions about the fiscal hedge and the pension bid, and the unanticipated increase in the linker share caused by unanticipated inflation this year. Executive Summary Thinner European credit supply remains a technical tailwind for spreads in 2026, but the direction of travel is turning. We expect supply growth will begin to pick up as capacity utilisation and fixed investment recover, the technology cycle broadens and the rates backdrop becomes less supportive of the cross-market funding dynamics that constrained reverse-Yankee supply this year. We do not expect a European tech supply tantrum: EU IG tech curves already offer ample steepness and screen cheap versus USD IG tech. However, a less mature market for longer maturity debt will mean that future EUR-denominated hyperscaler issuance is likely to require shorter maturities or meaningful concessions. 2026 marks the high point of Europe’s supply tailwind We expect European credit supply growth to pick up in 2027, making technicals less supportive than they have been this year. Year-to-date, benign/negative supply growth across European IG/HY (+2%/-5% vs. 2025 YTD) has been a tailwind for spreads, in line with our expectations and in contrast to the strong increase in US IG supply. For now, the factors behind this divergence remain in place: European capex and M&A activity are still lower than in the US, while cheaper US funding costs across most sectors continue to discourage reverse-Yankee issuance. records.text: BESS – Demand robust but macro-uncertainty/overcapacity looms Source: Citi Research, CABIA, BNEF, Benchmark Minerals ■ Global BESS demand remains robust led by growth in renewable installations, and the AIDC capex cycle. With rapid growth in solar/renewable power generation weighing on mid-day electricity prices, storage buildouts can facilitate smoothing. We forecast BESS output to grow 50% y/y to ~1TWh in 2026 and to grow by another 20% y/y in 2027. BESS growth has been underpinned by demand from utilities, residential and commercial sectors. Cell manufacturers have also repositioned their EV cell production lines to manufacture cells for the energy storage sector given the subdued EV demand particularly in China. We see global BESS installations growing from ~500GWh this year to ~950GWh by 2030 with output being higher than shipments owing to supply chain lags. ■ While we remain constructive on BESS demand, near-term risks stem from the structural overcapacity across the battery supply chain. Chinese regulators have expressed concerns and are reining in structural overcapacity by suspending construction of new energy storage cell projects ( Bloomberg, 11 th Sep). This, combined with global macro uncertainty and interest rate tightening may result in certain BESS projects either being delayed or pushed back. records.text: Lithium market moving to state of balance in 2027 Lithium – Market moving to a state of balance, however risks persist Source: Citi Research, Benchmark Minerals, Company Reports, Bloomberg We forecast the lithium market shifting to a modest surplus in 2027 (~19kt LCE, ~1% of supply) after a deficit of ~90kt LCE (~4% of supply) in 2026. However, delays to mine restarts and further policy tightening could easily swing the market back into deficit. The 2026 shortfall was driven by strong battery demand and supply constraints, including supply constraints in Zimbabwe and the delayed restart of JXW mine pushed back following an environmental review. On an unadjusted basis, we estimate mine supply growth of ~550kt LCE in 2027, led by China (~220kt) and Australia (~150kt), with the balance from Argentina, Chile and Africa. Key wildcards remain the JXW restart, lepidolite licensing in China and Zimbabwe's concentrate export ban. While the ban on export of concentrates by Zimbabwe is due to take effect on 1 st January 2027, most producers still lack downstream conversion capacity. Our base case assumes a pragmatic transition, with temporary export quotas extended through 1H’27 until conversion facilities are operational. 145 Prepared for Cayla Buettner

The political stability seen since 2022 might not be replicable, but broad-based expressions of fiscal prudence and resilient growth so far offer reassurance. We remain neutral on BTPs, with external risks tempering enthusiasm for further spread compression. Morgan Stanley organised an investor trip to Rome, meeting with politicians and representatives of major public offices. We report the feedback we collected in this note. Political stability could become less certain heading into the next election: The electoral reform and coalition negotiations ahead of the next elections dominated investor questions in Rome. A centre-right alliance including Futuro Nazionale (FN) would need to reconcile policy differences, while the centre-left still needs to settle on a common programme and leadership arrangements. Our discussions suggest caution in extrapolating the current government's longevity and political stability into the next legislature. Fiscal prudence remained a consistent message across our discussions. Feedback from representatives of major public offices and policy- makers pointed to confidence in meeting the 2.9% deficit target for 2026. records.text: India ETF investments to counter the higher duties’ drag on silver imports Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg Indian imports rose to 15moz in August, reducing silver premiums to ~1% in September Indian ETFs saw fresh inflows in the past three months following earlier liquidations India imports to decline in 2026 with destocking balancing the marketAs of August, India's YTD cumulative silver imports stood at ~76moz, down 24% y/y, as higher import duties compressed May–July imports to just 5moz versus 37moz in 2025. The resulting supply tightness pushed local premiums above 7% (30dMA, ex-duty) in July, despite resilient investment and industrial demand. Since April, silver ETFs have attracted net inflows of $495mn, partly offset by $223mn of May outflows, while industrial demand remains supported by solar manufacturing, defence, and electronics. Premiums have since eased to ~1% (30dMA, ex-duty) in September following stronger August imports of 15moz, with positive premiums pointing to seasonally healthy stocking ahead of the festival season. Nevertheless, elevated duties are likely to keep imports demand-matched, deferring meaningful restocking until duties are reduced. Even if Sep–Dec 2026 imports match 2025 levels of 118moz, full-year imports would still fall ~10% y/y. While an improving macro backdrop should support investment demand and drive silver prices higher in 4Q'26, elevated price levels are likely to trigger destocking, creating a further headwind for import volumes.

records.text: US Economic Presentation27 September 2026 ab 38 Source: BEA, BLS, Haver, UBS What next? More bumps in the road? The expansion rests on AI and the related wealth gains. We are now passing peak fiscal support to growth, and monetary policy tightening and fiscal policy turning to drag means the two will be working in the same direction for the first time in years. In contrast, we are past peak tariff impact on inflation and potentially peak energy shock inflation. Will energy prices fall back, or supply constraints rise? The labor market has been resilient, but details suggest more vulnerability than appreciated. If the AI investment or support for equities falters, the expansion itself would be at risk. The FOMC now appears headed toward further restraining the ex-AI economy. As a base case, we expect the FOMC to raise the Fed funds rate twice in 2026. We doubt that dampens the AI investment momentum, within which much of the investment is imported and not payments to domestic workers or income. Rate hikes will work to slow the rest of the economy. In the stylized scenario where US diesel inventories build at the 1.6mb/d pace of lost foreign net exports, we estimate that national US diesel storage would fill after 9-10 weeks, with the theoretical potential to fill storage more quickly as much of the empty storage is not near US Gulf Coast refineries.2 In reality, refinery cuts would pick up and diesel demand would edge up before hitting storage limits, which would prevent or delay hitting tank tops. As US diesel inventories near storage limits, downward pressure on diesel prices would intensify, potentially pushing diesel margins negative, while gasoline prices would likely rise further. Lower US diesel prices would compress overall US refining margins and likely incentivize US refiners to cut utilization, reducing US output not only of diesel but also of gasoline and jet fuel. records.text: We are neutral on cocoa prices and expect rangebound trading Source: ICCO, Industry Reports, Citi Research, *subject to revision; some figures may round Weather remains the primary source of upside risk for cocoa prices because several key producing regions are simultaneously facing weather patterns that could reduce yields and tighten supply. In Ivory Coast, rainfall during the August mini-dry season has been significantly below normal, with only 19mm received versus a long-term average of roughly 50mm. While current crop conditions do not yet warrant major production downgrades, a failure of seasonal rains to return in September could impair pod survival, delay pod setting, and ultimately reduce main-crop yields. At the same time, dry conditions in Indonesia associated with the developing El Niño are increasing the risk of lower production in 2026/27, while excessively wet conditions in Ecuador could boost disease pressure later this year through black pod and frosty pod rot outbreaks. Taken together, these weather developments point to a growing risk that current production forecasts prove too optimistic, particularly if El Niño strengthens further into Q4. records.text: TOPCon-to-BC transition emerging as a key headwind for silver demand Source: Citi Research, PV Magazine, PV Tech, Taiyangnews Continued net losses in 2026 mean that companies need capital to run current operations The solar industry's gradual transition from TOPCon towards Back Contact (BC) technologies is emerging as a key medium-term theme for silver industrial demand. LONGi's HPBC 2.0 and AIKO's ABC technologies are at the forefront of this shift, combining higher conversion efficiencies with significantly lower metallization requirements. Unlike conventional PERC and TOPCon cells, BC architectures eliminate front-side metalization. LONGi’s ACM uses copper-based metallization, reducing or eliminating silver usage. For now, BC modules remain concentrated in premium residential and commercial rooftop applications, while TOPCon continues to dominate utility-scale installations owing to its lower cost, mature supply chain and established bankability. TOPCon's transition was rapid and relatively seamless. We do not expect a similar trajectory for BC technology, as solar manufacturers remain caught between weak industry economics and the need for significant capital investment. The sector has endured nearly two years of depressed profitability, driven by persistent overcapacity, intense price competition. records.text: over proved detrimental to real income. Keeping real wages low facilitates selling goods and services cheaply, but we have yet to see evidence of such an approach making the economy as a whole more prosperous. This is unsurprising given that it was suppression of wage growth that drove currency depreciation and deterioration in Japan's terms of trade in the first place. Underlying driver has been corporate reluctance to hike wages: We conclude that explanations blaming anaemic real wage growth on worsening of Japan's terms of trade are correct inasmuch as deterioration in the terms of trade has shown up in price statistics in the form of sluggish real wage growth but incorrect to the extent that an exogenous shock is viewed as the sole culprit. The terms of trade have ultimately deteriorated so much only because so many Japanese firms have opted for a pricing strategy that relies on curbing wage growth and selling things cheaply to remain profitable. Sluggish real wage growth, depreciation of the currency in real terms and worsening of the terms of trade may be distinct concepts, but in essence are all just manifestations of the same underlying issue: workers have not been financially benefitting from productivity gains. It should thus be eminently clear that the Japanese economy's protracted malaise has stemmed from a skewing of the distribution of primary income as real wages have not been allowed to keep pace with productivity growth. records.text: n quantity of imports. So we opted to measure the amount paid for imports in terms of export volume. Our expression for the narrowly defined terms of trade (τ = Px/Pm) implies that the cost of real imports M denominated in export prices is M/τ, which means that net exports on a real income basis – allowing for income flows in either direction due to changes in the terms of trade – can be expressed as NX(GDI) = X−M/τ. A decline in the narrowly defined terms of trade (τ) boosts M/τ, meaning that more will need to be paid for a given level of import volume (real imports) and that real exports will accordingly decline on a real income basis as more income flows overseas. The amount of income that flows into or out of a country due to a change in its terms of trade is termed the gain or loss from trade, respectively, and defined as NX(GDI)−NX(GDP). Gain from trade = NX(GDI)−NX(GDP) = (X−M/τ) – (X−M) = M−M/τ = M (1−1/τ) What this says is that gains from trade will decline – or losses from trade will increase – if the terms of trade deteriorate. This, in turn, implies that even an improvement in the price competitiveness of exports due to higher import prices being absorbed via wage controls and other cost-cutting measures (that is, even yen weakening in real terms and/or a deterioration in the terms of trade) will not boost net exports on a real income basis unless it translates into a sufficiently large increase in export volume (real exports). records.text: 2 US Viewpoint | 28 September 2026 Taking stock of the elections Stephen Juneau BofAS stephen.juneau@bofa.com Julia Saravalle, CFA BofAS julia.saravalle@bofa.com With the midterms a little over one month away, the likeliest scenario according to experts we trust remains a split Congress with Republicans maintaining control of the Senate and Democrats winning the House. That said, Democrats have opened more pathways to flipping the Senate and prediction markets have a Democratic sweep as the most likely scenario. While redrawn congressional maps favor Republicans in the House with estimates suggesting redistricting netted Republicans 8-10 seats, history and polling currently favor Democrats. Republicans hold a slim majority (218 seats vs. 214) and historically the Presidents’ party loses an average of 24 House seats in the midterms (Exhibit 1). Democrats also have a margin of 8.7pts in the Real Clear Politics generic congressional ballot, like levels seen in 2018 when they netted 41 seats (Exhibit 2). Election experts don’t expect the same type of wave this year though, since there are far fewer truly competitive races. Indeed, the Cook Political Report only rates 22 seats as toss-ups currently and an additional 21 as lean Republican or lean Democrat. Still experts and prediction markets expect Democrats will gain control of the House. records.text: narrowly defined terms of trade also declined sharply from around the mid-1990s into the next decade (Figure 5). The narrowly defined terms of trade were more volatile over that period, as import prices soared due to rises in international commodity prices, but then stopped falling during the 2010s. Another decline was seen in 2022, as the Russia–Ukraine war triggered a surge in commodity prices, but we have since witnessed somewhat of a recovery. Here too it would be misleading to dismiss the deterioration in Japan's narrowly defined terms of trade as merely a reflection of exogenous factors. We say this because a rise in import prices (due to, say, yen depreciation and/or rising international commodity prices) will not cause the terms of trade to worsen if firms are able to hike their export prices sufficiently to offset such cost pressures. Put simply, the price ratio between imported goods and exported goods will hold steady if export prices rise to the same degree as import prices. For instance, Germany and France – which, like Japan, are heavily dependent on imported commodities – have suffered relatively modest deteriorations in their terms of trade (Figure 6). records.text: Utilities Are Preparing for Scarcity, Not Surplus Source : EIA, ESA, Citi Research The latest US and European utility data reinforce what we believe is becoming the defining feature of the uranium market: utilities are continuing to procure and diversify as if security of supply remains a strategic priority, despite inventories reaching their highest levels of the current cycle. European utility inventories have risen from 35.7ktU in 2022 to 42.5ktU in 2025, while US utility inventories increased from 102.4Mlb U3O8 in 2022 to 118.3Mlb in 2025. At the same time, procurement continues to exceed consumption, with EU deliveries reaching 14.7ktU in 2025 versus fuel-loading requirements of just 11.7ktU, while US utilities purchased 46.9Mlb U3O8 in 2025 against reactor requirements of roughly 40.9Mlb. US utility uranium purchases declined 16% YoY to 46.9Mlb U3O8 in 2025 from 55.9Mlb in 2024. We do not view this inventory accumulation as evidence of an oversupplied market. Rather, it suggests utilities are increasingly concerned about future availability of uranium and fuel-cycle services, and are willing to carry larger strategic inventories than at any point in recent years to protect against future disruptions. records.text: Our analysis suggests that slightly tighter financial conditions and higher oil prices should together be roughly a 0.4pp drag on GDP growth. The downgrade we have made to our forecast for the year, in part based on incoming data, is only slightly smaller than that, suggesting that the puzzle of economic resilience is smaller than it might appear at first. The economy’s slight outperformance relative to what we might have expected largely comes from consumer spending. At the start of the year, we forecasted consumption growth of 2.4% in 2026 Q4/Q4. Under the market and commodity price moves that actually materialized, our oil shock model implies a 0.6pp hit to that forecast, partially offset by a 0.2pp boost from higher equity prices in our wealth effects model, netting to an expected 2.0% growth in consumption this year. records.text: 28 September 2026 Fixed Income Blog Page 4 Deutsche Securities Inc. In one line, it was a week in which a strong economy, sticky inflation, resumed hikes and growing bond supply all worked at once. What was new was that yields no longer fell when oil did, and the view that a 5% Treasury yield marks the end of the low-rate era spread. Tokyo was closed throughout. On Thursday JGBs imported the move in a single session, with a near-parallel sell-off of +6bp in 2y, +10bp in 5y, +9bp in 10y (to 3.075%, the highest since 1996), +8bp in 20y and +7bp in 30y (Figure 4). We were meeting London investors in the middle of that sell-off. In that environment, overseas investors' view on yen rates was broadly neutral. With US and European yields being driven by their own central banks' resumed hiking cycles, yen rates sat in a position where the BoJ had already moved and where a 10y at 3% could be called neither clearly cheap nor clearly rich against a 5% Treasury and a 3.5% Bund, and few investors held a strong directional conviction. Neutrality has two implications. First, with directional positions light, the discussion naturally turned to relative value in the level and the curve, and one reason nobody pushed back on long 2y, the 5s20s flattener and paying the body of the 2-5-10 swap butterfly is that none of the three is a bet on the direction of yields. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures 28 September 2026 1 Japan: Real yen depreciation and worsening terms of trade to persist OUR KEY VIEWS  We expect real yen depreciation and Japan's worsening terms of trade to persist, with improving corporate earnings continuing to coexist with a sluggish macroeconomy, as firms focus on limiting wages rather than passing higher import costs through to export prices.  While this has improved the price competitiveness of Japanese goods and services overseas, export volumes have not increased sufficiently to offset the income outflows caused by worsening terms of trade.  The root cause of Japan's protracted economic stagnation remains a distortion in primary income distribution, as wages have failed to keep pace with productivity gains. Moreover, we see no signs of a significant shift in corporate wage-setting behaviour. Decomposing real wage: The failure of productivity growth to be reflected in real wages has often been attributed to Japan's worsening terms of trade, with many economists arguing that higher import costs and resulting rises in consumer prices have prevented modest increases in nominal wages from translating into greater real purchasing power. However, we contend that there is likely to be more to the story. In other words, while a ‘selling cheaply’ strategy might have made Japanese exports more competitive, it was unsuccessful in generating the volume effects needed to prevent net losses from trade (through drainage of income abroad). Weak yen strategy could end up backfiring for economic growth: The limitations of a strategy that relies on currency depreciation to fuel economic growth are evident. Japan's experience has shown that a deterioration in the terms of trade – due to, say, a weakening of the yen and/or a focus on keeping export prices low – can easily impede real income recovery for the economy as a whole. Although some firms might have been content to see their competitiveness improve as lower relative wages and relative prices effectively made Japanese goods and services cheaper to overseas buyers, the nation has failed to see any meaningful improvement in net exports on a real GDP basis, and an increase in losses from trade has moreover proved detrimental to real income. records.text: UK Economics 28 September 2026 Citi Research 2 Year-ahead inflation expectations increased again in September. Short-term inflation expectations increased further in September in the latest Citi/YouGov survey. Year-ahead inflation expectations were 4.5%, up from 3.9% in August. This has pushed the series back towards levels that we saw in Q2 2026 in the wake of the initial energy shock from Hormuz. On a three-month basis, year-ahead expectations have now reversed and are 3.9%, up from 3.7%. Like last month, the increase in expectations is broad-based with every subcategories recording an increase, with the largest jump in the Midlands at +82bps. The distribution of expectations also continues to worsen with 25% of respondents now expecting inflation above 6% in a year, up from 21% last month and 17% the month before. Similarly, the share expecting inflation below 2% has fallen to 10%, from 23% back in July. The latest DMP survey from the Bank of England for year-ahead expectations was 3% in August, where it was unchanged on the month before. Another DMP print is due later this week. The equivalent BoE/Ipsos result was 2.9% in July. Figure 1. Household short- and long-term inflation expectations © 2026 Citigroup Inc. No redistribution without Citigroup’s written permission. records.text: Commodities outlook – in the hands of the US President and Iran’s SNSC Source: Citi Research ■ The conflicts in the Middle East and Russia/Ukraine and the strengthening El Nino are combining to create inflationary shocks through energy and agricultural commodities prices, which are up 90% and 20% respectively over the year to date. These developments have driven up overall commodities prices by more than 30% year-to-date (per the Bloomberg Commodities Index). Global oil expenditures are estimated to be running over ~$5tr annualised at present (~4% of world GDP), up $2.5tr, and roughly double their ~$2.6tr level (~2% GDP) at the start of the year. Though this is clearly creating upward pressures on inflation, oil expenditures as a share of GDP remain around half of what they were during the height of the 2nd oil shock in the late 1970s (7-8% of GDP). ■ There are increasingly clear signs of stress in some major oil product markets, with products much more affected than crude oil markets by the recent shock (please see slides 7, 21, and our Special Section slides 18-28 for details). The Diesel/Gasoil/Heating Oil market has been particularly badly affected, which is important as it is the largest single oil product market accounting for ~30% of global oil demand, and a key component of global logistics/supply chains. As we enter Q4'26, significant maturity walls are approaching, forcing firms to refinance in a higher-rate environment while also facing impaired fundamentals and continued uncertainty stemming from AI-related disruption. In Figures 1 and 2, we highlight the current state of software maturity walls. There is $23.2 billion of leveraged loans and $4.3 billion of high-yield bonds due over the next two years, with an additional $37 billion and $9 billion, respectively, due within the following three years. As shown in the figures below, the maturity wall is heavily concentrated in Software $LL, so we examine the loan maturity wall in greater detail below. We typically analyze maturity walls on a rolling basis (T+1, T+2, T+3, etc.) rather than by calendar year. This approach avoids seasonality issues and better reflects the way rating agencies assess debt obligations. When bonds or loans fall below one year to maturity, the debt shifts from a long-term liability to a current liability on a company's balance sheet. This can affect financing ratios and potentially trigger rating actions. As we have highlighted previously, spreads often lead downgrades by one to two quarters; hence maturity-wall challenges can start negatively impacting spreads about 15 to 18 months before the actual maturity date. Some investors, on the other hand, gave little weight to the vote or to political constraints. Their view was that the only way to stop yen weakness is to keep hiking, and that the BoJ will keep hiking even if the successors to board members Takata and Tamura, whose terms end in July 2027, are appointed by the current administration from the cautious camp. It is a reading in which the durability of the hiking cycle is decided by the yen rather than by the composition of the Policy Board, and it shares a root with our own framing of the yen as part of the reaction function. Our answer is to think in terms of the terminal rate rather than the cadence. Our path has two further 25bp hikes, in January and April 2027, to a 1.75% terminal, and stops there. In Georgia and Texas, two other major data center hubs, local governments are pursuing moratoriums and zoning ordinances independently of state governments. As local jurisdictions move faster than state legislatures, developers face a more complex and less predictable regulatory environment. These developments could slow the pace of data center construction if they raise costs or cause firms to reconsider where they deploy capital. Nevertheless, states seeking to attract investment are likely to capitalize on restrictions imposed elsewhere. As a result, while regulation may influence the geographic distribution of data center investment, we expect its aggregate effect on economic growth over the next two years to remain limited. Two days of discussions in Rome left us with a clear message: the political stability experienced over the last 4 years could become less certain following the next elections. However, many participants expressed the view that fiscal prudence is likely to remain an important policy priority, irrespective of the coalition that emerges from the next election. Both officials and investors in Rome shared the view of a surprisingly resilient Italian economy, at least in the first half of 2026. The 2027 budget (the last one before the next election) may provide insight into the government's policy priorities heading into the campaign period. records.text: We are more bullish corn/soy/wheat In the near term Source: USDA, Bloomberg, Citi Research We revise our corn, wheat and soybean price forecast higher, as prices have reached our near-term targets, and now expect corn to reach $5.75/bu, wheat to reach $7.5/bu and soybeans to $13.5/bu over the next three months. Over a 12-month horizon, we expect corn prices to reach $6/bu, wheat prices to rise to $8/bu, and soybean prices to increase to $14.5/bu. Prices across the grains and oilseeds complex have rallied, driven by Black Sea trade disruptions, robust export demand, concerns over delayed corn and soybean planting in Brazil, and growing expectations for stronger biofuel demand. We do not expect this rally to be over and are revising our price forecasts higher as stock-to-use (STU) ratios continue to tighten. In our base case, we expect a resolution of the Black Sea disruptions during 4Q, which should help alleviate some of the pressure on global grain markets. However, even if trade flows normalize, we believe weather risks and expanding biofuel blending requirements will become the primary drivers of agricultural prices. What does the data tell us? Net exports on a real GDP basis tended to benefit from deterioration in Japan's terms of trade up until around 2007 (Figure 9), but have largely remained stagnant thereafter even when the terms of trade were worsening. Many seemingly accepted income outflows as the price of boosting net exports, but no such boost has been seen since around the end of the 2000s decade. So what about net exports on a real income basis after allowance for income outflows? This measure has also deteriorated since the late 2000s, when the terms of trade were worsening (Figure 10), which indicates that the Marshall–Lerner condition has not been satisfied in the context of the Japanese economy. In recent years, current account deficit financing has relied on foreign buying of gilts (see page 4, Figure 12) and we think this has contributed to a persistently positive GBP–gilt correlation (see page 4, Figure 13). The return of M&A inflows can reduce this sensitivity to foreign inflows into gilts, we think, and be a source of resilience for the GBP. Large, cheap public equity market drives high UK share of global cross-border M&A volume: This years’ rebound in UK M&A inflows reflects a global recovery in deal-making activity and the UK continuing to capture a sizeable share of these flows, we find. Global M&A volumes have been subdued in recent years amid repeated global shocks and tighter financial conditions. This year’s rebound appears to be a return to a more normal pace (see Figure 3) perhaps helped by corporates and private equity sharing our optimism on the global growth outlook (see Global Outlook Q4 2026, dated 8 September). The UK’s consistent ability to capture the second-largest share of cross-border M&A flows is structural, not cyclic

The market and London are faster than us on cadence, and the market is higher than us on the terminal; the 2y at 1.912% sits on top of that faster and higher path. The point that matters is that cadence barely moves the 2y; the terminal does. Whether the next hike comes in December or January is worth a few basis points to a 2y yield. So in London we did not dwell on December versus January and moved the discussion to the level: if the terminal is 1.75%, the 2y is a buy. Neither the December majority nor the investors arguing for a more hawkish BoJ objected, because their own terminal is 2% and the 2y already prices most of it. The premise of long 2y fails not on a faster cadence but on a repricing of the terminal to 2.25% or higher, which is the regime in which 50bp steps become plausible or the BoJ itself judges that underlying inflation is overshooting 2%. That is why the stop sits at 2.00%. This is also where we part company with the view that the BoJ will keep hiking to stop the yen. If hikes justified by the yen continue without waiting for underlying inflation to reach 2%, the terminal is repriced above 1.75% and the 2y moves toward the stop.
