records.text: Zinc – Neutral outlook with sensitivity to growth and mine supply outcomes Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg, Wood Mackenzie, ILZSG, BGRIMM, LME ■ In our base case (60% probability), we see zinc prices holding around current levels (~$4,000/t) near-term. While we see the physical market as relatively balanced into 2027 we think risks skew towards some moderation of elevated positioning and price in 2027 given zinc’s tepid longer-term structural demand exposure and the risk that mine supply or LME premium over SHFE eases. However, price action could be highly volatility given record investor positioning on both the long and short side; zinc is sensitive to both cyclical growth sentiment and mine supply growth expectations, the latter has proven very difficult to call over the last 18 months. ■ In our bull scenario (20% probability), prices climb to average $4,300/t in 4Q’26 and $4,500/t in 2027. This assumes zinc continues to trend higher either on cyclical demand recovery on a major pullback in energy prices and pickup in growth expectations. If energy costs in Europe spike significantly this could also prove bullish if smelters (e.g. in Europe) come under severe cost pressure as in late- 2020/2021. ■ In our bear scenario (20% probability), prices trend lower to average ~$3,000/t by end-2027 , as cyclical growth continues to underwhelm but mine supply recovers well, with a surplus (or expectations of oversupply) or broader negative risk sentiment prompting significant investor

records.text: Sugar rally has further to run, albeit some consolidation near-term Source: Citi Research, European Commission, GP, ISMA, TRS, UNICA, USDA, Industry Sources We remain bullish on sugar and reiterate our price targets of $0.19/lb over the next three months and $0.22/lb over the next 12 months, driven by a strengthening El Niño, and likely increased pull for diversion of sugarcane toward ethanol production. Supply risks continue to build across several key producing regions, while India's recent measures to contain domestic sugar prices, including authorizing 1mmt of duty-free raw sugar imports, releasing government stocks, and directing mills to divert additional sucrose toward sugar production, reinforce our view that domestic inventories are considerably tighter than officially reported. Below-normal rainfall across Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Marathwada increases downside risks to 2026/27 production, while sharply lower ethanol diversion highlights the severity of the underlying supply deficit. Beyond India, adverse weather conditions are also raising production risks in Thailand, further reducing global supply flexibility and reinforcing a constructive outlook for sugar prices. Brazil remains the market's key balancing supplier; however, weather-related operational and harvest execution risks during the remainder of the season leave little margin for error and could constrain export availability in the coming months. records.text: 6. Midterms move into view. With the midterm elections now barely a month away, we are having more conversations with investors about whether and how much they may matter to markets. That may play out again, but with a divided government, practical legislative policy shifts are likely to be small (even though foreign and trade policy volatility may continue). For instance, in the period leading up to the financial crisis (2004–07), investment grew on average at around 0.8% q/q, yet at different points within that period it contracted by nearly 1.4% q/q and expanded by as much as 7% q/q. This reminds us that while economic models provide smooth forecasts, they are more likely to capture the average of the forecasting window rather than an exact path for each quarter. Surveys are good, not perfect: On top of this, survey indicators are not always a direct proxy for q/q GDP prints. While the Ifo and composite PMI generally give a good guide of the direction of travel, they do not necessarily translate one-for- one to hard data observed in specific quarters. For instance, between 2013 and 2014 these surveys correctly captured the general improvement in the economic situation (a recovery from the sovereign debt crisis) but % q/q GDP figures displayed erratic behaviour. records.text: the upcoming end of the RRF was the main test of that resilience. The concern is straightforward: once the programme reaches its final stage in 2026, the disappearance of a large incremental spending impulse could weaken growth in 2027. The prevailing feedback was that some moderation is likely, but a sudden stop in investment is not inevitable. Domestic funding, local investment pipelines and the release of construction capacity previously absorbed by the Superbonus were among the potential cushions discussed. These mechanisms could at least in part smooth the transition. The more substantive reassurance on the concern about an abrupt correction in public investment was the intention expressed by officials to keep public investment elevated beyond the end of the programme. The final payment of the Italian RRF is worth €28.4bn, and it should be disbursed by the Commission by the end of 2026. The spending of this instalment should spill over into 2027, also allowing officials to cushion part of the correction from the end of the programme.

records.text: over proved detrimental to real income. Keeping real wages low facilitates selling goods and services cheaply, but we have yet to see evidence of such an approach making the economy as a whole more prosperous. This is unsurprising given that it was suppression of wage growth that drove currency depreciation and deterioration in Japan's terms of trade in the first place. Underlying driver has been corporate reluctance to hike wages: We conclude that explanations blaming anaemic real wage growth on worsening of Japan's terms of trade are correct inasmuch as deterioration in the terms of trade has shown up in price statistics in the form of sluggish real wage growth but incorrect to the extent that an exogenous shock is viewed as the sole culprit. The terms of trade have ultimately deteriorated so much only because so many Japanese firms have opted for a pricing strategy that relies on curbing wage growth and selling things cheaply to remain profitable. Sluggish real wage growth, depreciation of the currency in real terms and worsening of the terms of trade may be distinct concepts, but in essence are all just manifestations of the same underlying issue: workers have not been financially benefitting from productivity gains. It should thus be eminently clear that the Japanese economy's protracted malaise has stemmed from a skewing of the distribution of primary income as real wages have not been allowed to keep pace with productivity growth. On the back of higher energy prices, headline inflation moves higher to 3.2% (+10bp) in ’26, 3.2% (+60bp) in ’27 and to 2.0% (-10bp) in ’28. Core inflation moves to 2.8% (unch), 2.5% (+20bp) and 2.1% (unch) in ’26/27/28. The upside largely reflects recent and expected strength in core goods as higher energy costs gradually feed through. Underlying inflation remains broadly stable, with limited evidence so far that the energy shock has generated broad -based spillovers or second -round effects through wages. However, the longer energy prices remain elevated, the greater the risk for the inflation shock to become broader and more persistent. Our ECB call assumes one further 25bp hike in December, to a terminal rate of 2.75%. However, with inflation expected to rise quickly to 4% in Q4 -26 and economic activity proving resilient, the hawks may push to bring the hike forward to October. In our view, the absence of compelling evidence of indirect and second-round effects remains consistent with a quarterly pace of hikes. The risk is that the ECB has to hike to 3.0% if energy prices remain elevated and the perceived risk of energy inflation spilling over into core inflation rises. Hiking above 3 .0% would need either clear evidence of second -round effects , strong growth or the ECB to believe that the neutral rate is closer to 3% than 2%. records.text: Uncertainty over the composition of the centre-right coalition generates questions around the outlook for another Meloni government. Compared to just one year ago, the time of our last trip to Rome, there is now more uncertainty around the coalition's prospects of securing a second term. Participants frequently highlighted developments within the wider right as a key source of uncertainty for the continuity of the current government. Meloni's administration became the Republic's longest-lasting single government in September. Yet its prospects for a second term increasingly depend on the newly created party (Futuro Nazionale, FN) headed by former general Roberto Vannacci. Vannacci was elected to the European Parliament as a member of the League party, but earlier this year he created his own party, attracted politicians from the governing coalition parties and declared his party in opposition. The scale of the shift in the equilibrium within the Italian right is visible in the polls: FN is polling strongly at 8%, up meaningfully from the 3.6% registered in February. These numbers may help explain why a party outside Meloni's governing coalition has become relevant to calculations about its future. At broadly prevailing polling levels, bringing FN into the current centre-right coalition would make the 42% threshold much easier to reach. However, it was not clear to the panelists whether increased growth in stablecoins would contribute to new demand for Treasuries: on one hand, if this demand came from cash or from foreign assets, it would represent new sources of demand. The thermal coal market remains tight largely driven by supply disruptions. Supply-side risks remain elevated, including slower ramp up of Chinese domestic production owing to mine safety inspections, Indonesian production quotas, and diesel shortages. Demand for coal in the Northern hemisphere is likely to be dampened by Super El Niño (milder winter). However, we do see scope for winter restocking by utilities across North Asia, albeit at a lower level. records.text: ab 28 September 2026 Global Research US Equity Strategy Rates spike and equities: what's next? P/E derating has been large amid surge in 10yr As the US 10yr yield has risen ~100bp YTD, with a ~50bp spike in the last month, the S&P 500 NTM P/E has fallen 17% since Nov. The P/E derating is nearing recession/ slowdown levels of 20%+ and is in line with the 1994 Fed cycle derating. While there have been many drivers of the 10yr rise, the shift from expectations of Fed cuts last fall to now pricing more Fed hikes has likely been the main driver, with 1y1y rates up ~180bp since Nov-Dec. SPX has rallied 10% on avg in the year following a rates spike with much stronger 18% avg rallies when the Fed did not raise rates >1pp within a year. Inflation expectations have been elevated but contained, which makes a benign Fed hike path and further SPX upside likely assuming no breakout in inflation/employment. SPX path likely driven by Fed path post historic 10y yield spike The US 10yr has surged to 5.2%, over 80bp above the 1yr moving average and a z-score of 1.6. The 10yr has cleared +1.5 stdev above its 1yr moving average only seven times in 40 years. Many catalysts will affect the path of rates (oil, employment, inflation prints, midterms), but 10y yields did not meaningfully decline for 2+ months post this stage of10yr spikes, and yields increased further in full Fed hiking cycles.  Fed hikes moderate -> equities rallied. records.text: We model the effects on diesel and gasoline prices from potential restrictions on n US diesel exports—a very plausible scenario, though not our base case—and draw five conclusions. First, a diesel export ban would initially likely put moderate downward pressure n on US diesel prices as inventories build. We estimate that, initially while storage remains available, each week of a US diesel export ban would be associated with $0.25/gallon of downward pressure on average US retail diesel prices, or just under 4% of the current $6.5/gallon. Second, the longer a diesel export ban lasts, the more disruptive it would likely n be by putting upward pressure on gasoline prices because diesel, gasoline, and jet fuel are largely produced together. Therefore, downward pressure on diesel production can mean downward pressure on gasoline production, i.e. upward price pressure on gasoline. As US diesel stocks near storage limits, downward pressure on diesel prices would intensify, compressing US refining margins, and likely incentivize US refiners to reduce output. We estimate that, once diesel storage is full, each week of a US diesel export ban would likely be associated with $0.3/gallon of upward pressure on US retail gasoline prices. Third, restrictions on US diesel exports would add upward pressure on ex-US n diesel prices. records.text: ~15% of 2027* supply at risk of delays/policy induced restrictions Lithium – ~16% of supply at risk of further delays/policy restrictions Source: Citi Research, Benchmark Minerals, Bloomberg, Company Reports *on an unadjusted basis Our neutral stance on lithium reflects elevated uncertainty around the 2027 supply outlook. As discussed previously, the key swing factors remain the restart of China's JXW mine, ongoing lepidolite licensing reviews in Jiangxi, and Zimbabwe's concentrate export ban. Collectively, we estimate that 16% of global LCE supply faces potential disruption from restart delays and policy-related risks. Zimbabwe, which accounts for ~7% of global LCE supply, is set to implement its concentrate and ore export ban from 1 st January 2027. With no formal resolution in place and the deadline approaching, our base case assumes a 3-6 month implementation delay to allow producers additional time to commission downstream conversion capacity. Failure to grant an extension would tighten market balances materially. Elsewhere, further delays to the JXW restart, which remains under environmental review, would weigh on supply, while additional licensing scrutiny across Jiangxi's lepidolite operations presents further downside risk. Our base case assumes JXW restarts in 4Q’26 and ramps up through 2027, with other lepidolite mines continuing to operate. We also incorporate a disruption allowance of ~150kt LCE, equivalent to ~6% of global supply. 146 Prepared for Cayla Buettner

This shows that even if productivity (a) rises, in the absence of growth in the real wage (ω) we will see a decline in labour's income share (λ), a deterioration in the terms of trade (θ) or quite possibly both. Japan's broadly defined terms of trade deteriorated from the mid-1990s into the next decade (Figure 3), and some might reasonably assume that this was a factor behind declines in the real wage over the same period. But the terms of trade were not worsening during the 2010s, when real wages remained stagnant even as productivity improved, suggesting that the main culprit was instead a decline in labour's share of income (Figure 4). In other words, the primary issue during the 2010s was not a deterioration in Japan's terms of trade, but rather a distribution mechanism that did not allow workers to adequately benefit from their improved productivity in the form of higher real wages. records.text: Thermal Coal – We see tight fundamentals easing next year Source: Citi Research, Wood Mackenzie, Bloomberg ■ Seaborne thermal coal demand in the near term is likely to be supported by import demand from India and parts of Asia. However, we expect seaborne thermal coal demand to see structural decline over the medium term. We expect Chinese imports to show sequential growth, reflecting tight domestic supply following heightened mine safety inspections after the Shanxi mine accident in May 2026. While policymakers continue to prioritize energy security through higher domestic production, we do not expect a meaningful acceleration in output over the remainder of the year, with China's raw coal production down 4% YTD (8M’26). In India, we expect import demand to strengthen into 4Q’26 as low power plant inventories drive restocking requirements. Although India remains focused on increasing domestic coal production, recurring weather and logistics disruptions continue to create regional supply dislocations, sustaining the need for imports. ■ Seaborne thermal coal supply this year remains constrained by a range of operational and geopolitical disruptions with exports to be down 4% y/y in CY’26. records.text: 4. Easier to see paths to some rate relief from current levels. Stepping back, the rise in long-end yields continues to be driven by higher real rates to a large extent. Alongside the resilient nominal growth environment that is pushing central banks to hike again, a big part of the story of higher real rates is the confluence of high fiscal deficits with increased corporate sector demand for capital to finance the AI investment boom. Until that boom fades, upward pressure on real rates is likely to persist and overly dovish central bank policy may simply transfer pressure from the front to the back of the yield curve. But with more inflation risk and more policy rate tightening now priced, there are more obvious paths than before to some relief (and even more to stability) in the back end, even if growth remains solid. The quickest path to relief would be a meaningful decline in energy prices, which would reduce the front-end risk premium. More benign core inflation outcomes may eventually deliver the same result, but more slowly. Any sign of increasing pressure on consumers—signaling that tightening and energy pressures are biting—could also dampen rate concerns. But we think that relief is likely to have limits, especially at the longer end of the curve, unless the growth or AI spending outlook softens meaningfully. A very short primer on the new electoral law The current government is aiming to replace the "Rosatellum" mixed system (broadly speaking 63% proportional, 37% first-past-the-post), with the "Stabilicum": proportional representation with a majority premium to the party or coalition that comes first and wins at least 42% of the votes. The proposed system makes coalition arithmetic particularly important. A leading list or coalition reaching at least 42% of the vote in both chambers would receive a majority bonus of up 70 deputies and 35 senators, ~17% of the seats in both houses, enough to guarantee a majority in Parliament. If no party/coalition were to reach the 42% share of votes threshold, the allocation of seats would be proportional (we don’t dwell on thresholds, for representations for simplicity). The text also requires parties or coalitions to identify their proposed Prime Minister when registering. For investors, the relevant question is therefore not simply who comes first, but given the fragmentation of the Italian political landscape, whether the winner of the next election will have a result strong enough to obtain the majority premium, and hence a workable parliamentary majority. Uncertainty over the composition of the centre-right coalition generates questions around the outlook for another Meloni government. BoJ: the question was cadence, not level Almost every BoJ question in London was about what comes next. At its 17-18 September meeting the BoJ raised the policy rate to 1.25%, the highest since April 1995 and, at three months after the June move, the shortest interval of this cycle. Investors had already moved on: would October's 29-30 meeting bring a back-to- back hike, does December take the rate to 1.50%, and is the terminal 2%? The majority answer was clear: as long as the yen stays at 157 to 159, the next hike is in December. Few made October their base case, and fewer still asked about 50bp steps. Behind those questions sits the 7-2 vote. The two dissenters, board members Asada and Sato, were both appointed under the current administration, and the currency market read the split as a political constraint on the pace of hikes and sold the yen. Some in London read it the opposite way, as a board that brought the hike forward over the objections of two members, but the view we have heard since July, that the BoJ is behind the curve and will lose the bond market's confidence unless it accelerates, remains widely held. This is in line with our view that the recent steepening of US IG credit curves reflects investors reassessing ROI and monetization risks rather than supply indigestion. While excess steepening in EU IG tech curves vs. EU IG non-tech has been around 30-40% of that seen in US IG this year, this is broadly consistent with the ~45% issuer overlap between the two markets. We also disagree with the view that USD supply is commanding a persistent indigestion premium. records.text: Strong El Niño and weather implications for grains/oilseeds Citi Research ■ A Super El Niño poses significant upside risks to corn, wheat, and soybean prices through its impact on yields across several key producing regions. For corn, the primary risk is hotter and drier conditions in Southeast Asia, Southern Africa, and parts of Australia, while weather disruptions in South America can delay planting and negatively impact crop development. Although parts of the US Corn Belt may initially benefit from improved moisture conditions, a strong El Niño often increases weather volatility globally and raises the risk of production shortfalls outside North America. ■ For wheat, the risks are particularly pronounced in Australia, one of the world's largest exporters. Historically, strong El Niño events have been associated with below-trend Australian wheat yields due to hot and dry conditions during critical growing stages. Additional risks include dryness across parts of Southeast Asia and potential weather stress in portions of the Black Sea region, tightening exportable supplies and increasing competition among importers. ■ For soybeans, the greatest concern centers on South America, particularly Brazil and Argentina. A strong El Niño can lead to excessive rainfall in some regions, delaying planting, disrupting fieldwork, and increasing disease pressure, while other areas may experience periods of heat and moisture stress. This is based on: 1. The absence of additional pro-growth fiscal policies; 2. The prospect for lower rates amid less reflationary policies and a potentially bearish equity market backdrop; 3. According to the Chinese commerce ministry over 90% of the products are intended to receive Most Favored Nation tariff rates. Our forecasts see core inflation at ~2.7% on average next year, and market implied ex-energy inflation is around 3% in H2 2027 (Figure 9), an upward revision of more than 1pp since February. Valuations incorporate much of the supportive macro backdrop; at the 1y point, market pricing is around 30bp above our HICP forecasts, suggesting some embedded risk premium , while front-end forwards are close to the upper end of this year’s range. Morgan What does this mean for options markets? Given the current levels of implieds and the current jump frequency, markets have to deliver less on non-jump days to break even (Fig- ure 9). For example, given a 10% jump frequency for 2-year tails, they need to deliver about 6bp on non-jump days for positions to break even. This number decreases significantly as the jump frequency increases, creating a risk to short-gamma positions. Therefore, as we approach NFP next week, and with geopolitical uncertainty still in the background, we recommend patience before initiating outright shorts even at these levels. However, for investors who would like to initiate shorts, we recommend anchoring them in 30-year tails, as 30-year tails have been delivering the least amount of volatility on non-jump days and have a lower jump frequency than the other tails . We prefer pairing shorts in 6M expiries with longs in 1Y expiries, vega-neutral, for soft bearish gamma exposure in 30-year tails. Additionally, the implied vol differential has declined substantial- ly this week and is near YTD highs ( Figure 10 ). Therefore, we recommend selling 6Mx30Y straddles versus buying vega-neutral 1Yx30Y straddles, delta hedged daily (see Trade recommendations ). The energy shock may yet still be a drag but we see it as modest from a growth standpoint still, though risks are increasing. The energy shock is adding some basis points to forward core inflation forecasts, hence also contributing to the higher Fed policy. At a global level, the growth impulse is increasingly capex and manufacturing-led, with Asia at the center. Growth momentum in the region is holding very well, supported by AI demand and a broader capex cycle tied to energy security, defense spending, and supply-chain reconfiguration. Chinese growth remains K-shaped, with industrial and export momentum improving while domestic demand remains uneven. In the euro area, we expect that real growth will continue to be strong, driven by resilient exports and positive public investment - these offset soft domestic private investment. records.text: 10. Protected upside. Although the ongoing risks from the same three macro factors that have dominated recent months are unresolved, we see clearer upside paths than before, as those risks have been more obviously priced. The simplest of those paths run through some reversal in oil and rate fears, particularly as growth pricing is still quite solid. By the same token, intensification of oil and rate pressures are still the biggest risk and remain quite easy to envisage. While the macro backdrop remains complicated, we think it makes more sense to position for higher equities than it has for a little while, particularly since options markets are making it easier to do that in protected forms. The broad environment has also remained carry-friendly, despite the bumps. We still favour diversifying equity risk (across the pieces of the AI complex, and beyond it), to “internalize” the volatility that comes from shocks that affect the distribution of winners and losers across those groups. The pricing of DM front-end rate markets is starting to look more stretched as the market incorporates both more extended hiking cycles and higher rates for longer. But with assets still vulnerable to energy risks and a more front-loaded hike path, this particular opportunity may better suit investors with long horizons or diversified portfolios at this point. records.text: 5. A better short-term runway for equities, despite the risks. Earnings remain impressively strong across geographies, supported by the AI boom and high nominal growth. With a higher share of GDP growth than normal finding its way to profits, companies are likely “over-earning” relative to a long-term trend, though our US equity strategists still expect solid though slower growth in earnings for 2027 and 2028. With the market de-rating across the AI complex in recent months, and forward P/E multiples falling, the bar for upside surprises is lower as we head towards the Q3 earnings season. The main downside risks to equities remain the same—higher energy prices, another push higher in rates or a bump in the AI narrative. But with all three risks better priced than a month ago, it has been easier to identify an upside path for equities too, especially since the September FOMC. The Nasdaq has led the recent bounce, highlighting the reduced positioning and greater worry in the tech complex lately, although there are some signs of rebuild in hyperscaler length recently. Oil and rate shocks have continued to weigh on cyclical areas sensitive to those pressures (transports, housing) but could help to drive a rally in an oil relief scenario. Though it is hard to say how it may shape economic policy, Democrats could also effectively control nominations in our baseline scenario if the Senate is split 50-50. This is because historically the Senate has evenly divided members on the Committees that confirm presidential nominations. Democrats could also attempt to use reconciliation to eliminate planned Medicaid cuts, expand Affordable Care Act subsidies, and offset those measures through some form of higher corporate tax rates, an elimination of full expensing, and/or higher individual taxes. That said, we would expect the President to veto a bill of this design, and Democrats might prefer to keep these policy goals as part of its 2028 platform. Additionally, a Democratic sweep likely means better down-ballot performance. We would expect a wider margin in the House for Democrats relative to our baseline, which will make the caucus easier to manage and moderate policy goals. It would also translate to more Democratic wins at the Gubernatorial and state legislature level too. That could potentially hasten passage of the AI/data center

records.text: met. ▪ Despite headwinds from domestic political uncertainty and the energy shock, we think the German economy will remain resilient and we expect above-potential GDP growth of 1.3% in 2027 supported by defence spending and the global AI buildout. ▪ Politics is unlikely to have an immediate effect on fiscal policy or the economy but sharpens risks around the post-2027 outlook. Spending set to continue: Cumulative monthly data shows that as of end-August, combined core and off-budget defence spending was at 53% and investment spending at 51% of the 2026 full-year target. While lower than the 67% implied by a linear disbursement, we do not see this as a concern. Historical data shows spending tends to be backloaded: on average, over 2019– 2025, 47% of final (core budget) investment spending and 40% of defence spending was delivered in the last four months of the year. Electoral blow: CDU underperformance in recent state elections has raised the risk of a renegotiation of parts of the coalition deal with the SPD and a potential shift towards spending with a lower fiscal multiplier, like tax relief. Our base case (60% probability) is for a recovery in silver investment demand, driving silver to $75/oz over the next three months, with early signs of improving sentiment already visible in strengthening ETF holdings and India ETF inflows. Silver has been under pressure of elevated oil prices, firmer inflation expectations, and markets pricing in Fed rate hikes, with a stronger US dollar and higher real rates adding further weight on precious metals. As policy expectations shifted hawkish, global silver ETFs recorded ~64moz of outflows YTD, while managed money net length collapsed to ~65moz from ~200moz a year ago, highlighting historically light investor positioning. We expect global silver ETF outflows to narrow to just ~10moz for full-year 2026, implying net inflows of ~75moz in 4Q'26 alone. Neither change means more JGBs; both mean holding them differently, and the market implications are quite different. A wider band only enlarges the room for benchmark buying concentrated in 1y to 10y, whereas a longer duration reaches the super-long sector for the first time. On our rough arithmetic, extending duration by one year means moving JPY5trn to JPY6trn from 3y into 30y, which adds a buyer of the 20y leg and is supportive for the 5s20s flattener. GPIF holding longer is both more likely, and more consequential for the curve, than the GPIF buying more JGBs that London was hoping for. What matters for the market is the maturity of that buying. GPIF's domestic bond holdings track a benchmark concentrated in the 1y to 10y sector (about 70% of NOMURA-BPI matures within ten years), and in the quarter in which it bought JPY5.7trn the 20y yield still rose 37bp. GPIF is not a put for the super-long sector, and that was the single most effective counterargument we made in London. records.text: Import duties remain a headwind for India gold imports through 2H’26 Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg We expect 2026 India gold imports to remain well below 2025 levels despite stronger Sep-Nov seasonality, reflecting high import duties and increased recycling. Pressure on FX reserves and the current account is likely to persist with oil prices above ~$100/bbl. India gold demand typically peaks in 4Q, with imports generally rising after June and building through November. However, higher import duties and increased recycling are likely to temper the seasonal recovery in 2026. Negative local premiums, averaging -1.6% in August 2026 and -1% MTD in September, following -1.2% in July, point to weaker import demand. Assuming September imports match July 2026 levels, and imports during the remainder of 2026 follow normal seasonality in line with 2025, total imports would reach ~15moz, implying an 8% decline y/y. We expect imports to rebound in 1Q’27 post potential SoH resolution in 4Q’26 and subsequent import duty reversal. The Ministry of Finance's issuance cuts and a stronger yen via intervention and hikes are the brakes on that risk, and the 180bp stop is the level at which the brakes come off: the regime we described in August as the unpriced put, fiscal dominance in which the BoJ is asked to buy with nothing in return. The 2-5-10 swap trade breaks the curve into three forward segments, 1y1y, 2y3y and 5y5y, pays the body (2y3y) and receives both wings. It puts belly-led bear flattening into a single trade: the 2y to 5y forward segment is where extra issuance lands and sells off most readily, the 1y1y wing is already capped by the priced terminal, and the 5y5y wing is anchored by life insurer buying and the Ministry of Finance's issuance cuts. Converting the 24 September closes from cash par yields into forwards, the body sits 20 to 30bp below the average of the wings (the range reflects the assumed swap spreads to cash), and the gap closes as the belly cheapens. In London many investors preferred this expression to the cash 5s20s flattener, because it is lighter on carry and is executed entirely in swaps, and it was accepted by neutral investors as well because it takes no view on direction. To avoid double-counting the same view, we present it as an alternative to the cash flattener rather than an addition. records.text: 2 China Watch | 28 September 2026 Leaders’ summit generated a shorter than expected truce The Trump-Xi summit delivered less than expected on trade, but more than expected on diplomatic signaling. The main outcome on trade was a two-month extension of the existing truce to January 10, well short of our expectation of a one-year extension. The short rollover likely reflects two factors. First, the two-month timeframe appears more closely aligned with the US position, allowing the US to assess China’s implementation of the existing agreement, particularly on rare-earth supplies. China did not specify the extension’s duration in its official statement, in contrast to its explicit disclosure of the one-year suspension following the 2025 leaders’ summit. Jamieson Greer also linked uncertainty over the extension to insufficient Chinese supplies of strategic minerals. Second, the two sides may simply need more time to negotiate. As Exhibit 2 shows, the September 24 leaders’ meeting followed only one formal negotiating round in New York, held four days earlier, compared with five negotiating rounds over roughly five months ahead of the October 2025 Busan summit. The shorter extension therefore gives both sides time to negotiate a broader agreement, with potential leader-level meetings at APEC in Shenzhen and the G20 in Miami offering additional opportunities to reach a deal before year-end. While some goods categories are naturally more exposed than others, much of the consumer basket is insulated because services account for such a large share of spending. We also find that diesel prices are not especially useful in explaining movements in core inflation or, somewhat surprisingly, core goods inflation. By contrast, diesel does exhibit some explanatory power for headline inflation and food prices. To evaluate these relationships, we use a simple OLS framework in which year-over-year inflation is the dependent variable. The key explanatory variable is the year-over-year change in diesel prices. We also control for lagged inflation, one-year-ahead inflation expectations, and an estimate of the output gap. The regressions are estimated over two samples: 1985 through the latest available observation and 1985-2019. The results for headline inflation are unsurprising given the correlation between diesel and gasoline prices. Our estimates suggest that a 1% increase in diesel prices is associated with roughly a 1-2 basis point increase in headline inflation. The results for food inflation are also intuitive. Transportation costs play an important role in food supply chains, while diesel prices tend to move alongside other agricultural inputs such as fertilizer. records.text: 14 US Viewpoint | 28 September 2026 Treasury supply creates a meaningful risk that the selloff broadens into the long end and ultimately becomes a bear steepening. FX Alex Cohen, CFA BofAS Much of what the FX market will learn from the US midterms may be more relevant to the 2028 outlook and beyond, than to any immediate economic ramifications of the election outcome. Current narratives mainly center around a Democrat controlled congress as being USD- negative on back of presumed lower growth, lower interest rates, and a potentially enhanced regulatory regime for AI-related firms. Meanwhile, a Republican sweep is generally seen as presenting a continuation of reflationary policies lower regulatory risks to AI and a higher interest rate regime, which would likely further support the USD. We see more scope for nuance for the USD, and would expect FX moves to be limited in any of the election scenarios, consistent with rate expectations outlined above. Historically, Dem. midterm “win” = downside USD risks Looking at past election outcomes is a useful yet flawed endeavor. Sample sizes are small and each backdrop is unique. Since 1980, there have been 5 midterm elections which the Democrats were considered to have “won” during a Republican administration. On average, these episodes do show modest USD depreciation in the ensuing two months (~-2%), though incidentally when the Democrats won the 2018 midterm of President Trump’s first term, the DXY was largely unchanged. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures 28 September 2026 3 So why is Japan worse off? The answer is that Japanese firms have taken a very different approach to pricing than their German and French counterparts, opting not to hike export prices even when import costs are rising and focusing instead on limiting wage expenses to remain profitable. Unit labour costs have effectively been kept under control by restricting increases in nominal wages even when productivity has improved, thereby enabling firms to stay in the black without needing to offset higher import costs by raising export prices. It should thus be clear that a deterioration in Japan's narrowly defined terms of trade is not simply an exogenous phenomenon attributable solely to higher import prices. Much of the time, it has been due to firms limiting their wage outlays to keep selling their products cheaply even when import costs have been rising. To put this another way, while the terms of trade might at first glance appear to be a neutral indicator of relative prices, they are actually liable to be heavily influenced by the behaviour of Japanese firms if wage suppression is used as the primary strategy for maintaining price competitiveness and profitability. In summary, both broadly and narrowly defined terms of trade have deteriorated due to a combination of exogenous import price shocks and corporate strategies that prioritise profit margins over productivity-linked

records.text: th broadly and narrowly defined terms of trade have deteriorated due to a combination of exogenous import price shocks and corporate strategies that prioritise profit margins over productivity-linked wage increases. Japan's terms of trade deterioration and real yen depreciation: There is a similar background to the recent declines in the yen's real exchange rate to levels lower than even those seen in the early 1970s, which have of course made Japanese goods, services and labour increasingly cheap by international standards. Productivity has been improving, but unless those gains are reflected in wages, the resultant lack of upward pressure on unit labour costs is liable to depress both wages and prices in relative terms, thereby further eroding the yen's real value. While many may blame the yen's sharp depreciation over the past few years on the Bank of Japan’s tardiness in hiking its policy rate, it appears that Japan's continuing currency weakness needs to be attributed to more than just financial factors such as interest rate differentials. A decline in the real exchange rate is not necessarily synonymous with deterioration in the terms of trade, but in the case of Japan, both have often happened simultaneously in what might be considered different expressions of the same economic phenomenon. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures The re-emergence of energy price concerns has driven terminal pricing for the ECB to move towards 3.50%. We believe that significant stop-losses have been triggered in both front-end long positions and curve steepeners over recent weeks. Attempts to fade these moves in linear space is complicated by a volatile and headline-driven market which remains focused on geopolitical developments in the Middle East. We therefore look towards an option expression that allows us to hold a 10s30s curve steepening view through the near-term erratic price action and allow our expected structural curve steepening factors to fully materialise (discussed in more detail here). We particularly highlight our expectations that curve-paying needs from Dutch pension funds remain significant for the January 2027 transition cohort (see Paying needs decline but curve needs still sizeable, dated 8 September). While implied volatility on 10s30s has risen significantly in the past month (see Figure 1) we don’t view the level as prohibitive, given our view that the curve could steepen aggressively if the conflict in the Middle East de-escalates and transition pre-hedging flows begin. Further, the downward sloping 10s30s forward curve (Figure 2) cheapens the cost of buying caps on a steeper curve. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures Fig. 3: Implied versus realised vol ratio (21 bd) Source: BNP Paribas Fig. 1: Implied vol 1 year percentile Source: BNP Paribas As the European rates market is currently a by-product of movements in the energy markets, where uncertainty remains extremely high, implied rates vol is close to the one-year peak. Despite implied volatility in the top-left being at the peak of the one-year range, due to the ferocity of front-end re-pricing in yields, implied vol here still remains below recent realised volatility. While this makes implied vols in the top-left appear optically cheap, at the current implied daily move of almost 7bp, the hurdle to further gains appears high and breakeven levels at expiry seem unattractive, in our view. We currently hold a short vol and long rates position in this part of the grid via our sale of ERZ7 puts (see Fading front-end pricing only in listed options, dated 14 September). We view an extension of the positioning-driven rises in front-end yields and implied vol as the main risk to our view.

records.text: ARCH Scenario 1: split congress In 2026, a Democrat controlled House & Republican controlled Senate is our base case: under such gridlock, the scope is limited for major new fiscal legislation. As a result, debt-limit and shutdown headlines, rather than a durable repricing of growth or inflation, should be the main sources of volatility. However, above-target inflation, a significantly larger deficit and a heavier Treasury-supply burden could mute any conventional gridlock-driven rally. Historically, split Congress produced limited immediate moves: yields rose 0.7bp in 2Y, fell 1.2bp and 0.45bp in 5Y and 10Y, and rose 5.55bp in 30Y 1D after the election, although QE2 influenced the long end. Scenario 2: Democratic sweep A Democrat sweep would introduce bull-steepening risk, although the move would depend more on risk sentiment than on an immediate change in fiscal policy. A sweep could support USTs if concerns about tighter oversight or AI / tech regs weaken equity sentiment. UST rally would likely be led by front end if risk-off move increases Fed easing expectations. The sole historical observation since 2002, the 2006 midterm, saw yields fall across the curve 1D after (2Y: -1.7bp, 5Y: -2.2bp, 10Y: -2.2bp, 30Y: -2.7bp). Unlike 2006, Democrats would face a Republican president and potential veto; constraining legislation makes prospective AI or technology restrictions more rhetorical than immediately binding. records.text: funded. That will keep nominal discretionary spending roughly flat in nominal terms at ~$1.9tn (5.8% of GDP) but slightly negative in real terms. It also makes the risk of a shutdown highly likely; however, the negative impact from a shutdown is temporary and quickly reversed in most instances. The debt-limit fight could begin as early as next May with the X-date likely in November according to Katie Craig of our rates strategy team (see report: US Rates Alpha: Debt limit, 8 Sep 26). This will give House Democrats leverage to extract a more meaningful policy goal. That could be a reduction in the planned cuts to Medicaid or a resumption of expanded ACA credits. But we think Democrats may opt for more of a symbolic win and wait to make healthcare a key aspect of the platform in the 2028 presidential election. AI and data center regulation rhetoric to pick up We also expect the negative rhetoric around AI and in particular data center construction to increase over the next two years should Democrats flip the House. In fact, it likely will pick up no matter the outcome if the recent House vote on the Ratepayer Protection Act is any indication. Democratic sweep: looks a lot like the baseline We do not expect a Democratic sweep to produce materially different economic outcomes relative to our baseline scenario. There will be limited legislation, AI/data center rhetoric may be even louder, and the administration will still focus on broad foreign policy and deregulation. The key differences are that Democrats would control the Senate confirmation process and could use reconciliation legislation to place bills on the President’s desk. Control over nominations could modestly slow the regulatory agenda, but not to an extent that would meaningfully alter the growth trajectory over the next two years. Democrats would be able to prevent the President from stacking the Fed Board with his picks should any governors leave. Powell is the only governor that must leave before the next Presidential election.

All in all, while the last-minute additions could weaken program stringency, CCA prices still rallied in May/June as policy certainty improved and 2027 remains a likely first year of deepening deficits. Japan's broadly defined terms of trade deteriorated from the mid-1990s into the next decade (Figure 3), and some might reasonably assume that this was a factor behind declines in the real wage over the same period. We think this level of inflows may continue, given a return to normality in global M&A activity, from subdued levels, and the structural nature of the UK’s high share of cross-border flows. Our findings suggest UK M&A inflows could settle at a durably higher run-rate of USD26bn per quarter (see Figure 2). We view this estimate as conservative and sufficient to help reduce the sensitivity of the GBP to gilts. Higher US exports, weaker Chinese imports, rerouted Gulf supply, inventory draws, and strategic reserve releases kept crude flowing and prevented widespread production cuts. Those buffers are now diminished, meaning we expect to see the next wave of energy shocks in producer prices. Early signals are visible: pressure is building toward the upstream end of the production chain: chemical PPIs have accelerated materially across Korea, Japan, Canada, and Europe, while rubber and plastics are beginning to follow. PPI will not directly mean CPI moves higher, but it is the first step – how margins and demand adjust become highly consequential in the final CPI transmission. Food inflation is in focus because of El Niño. Changing weather patterns can affect harvests, which are further exacerbated in the current environment by rising fertilizer prices. The direct relationship between local weather and domestic inflation is modest and highly uneven. The clearest price effects are concentrated in edible oils and tropical commodities rather than major grains, and the response builds only after several quarters. Our terminal remains the same, but we expect to reach it later. Risks to our view are balanced. A meaningful drop in energy prices due to a lasting deescalation or big downside data surprises can weaken the case for tightening and allow for one or no hike. records.text: What about the effect of higher oil and refined products prices? Our rule of thumb implies that a sustained $10/barrel increase in oil prices lowers GDP growth by just over 0.1pp through the consumption channel as higher energy costs erode real purchasing power. Applied to the path oil prices have taken this year, the unusual widening in refined product spreads, and our commodities strategists’ forecasts for prices through year-end, the rule of thumb implies a 0.4pp drag on GDP growth. While US oil producers were initially reluctant to respond to higher prices by increasing capex because of the uncertainty of the war with Iran and the outlook for oil prices, the increase in the rig count index in Q3 (Exhibit 3) points to a pickup in energy capex more recently. We estimate that the consumption drag and capex boost will net out to a 0.3pp hit to GDP growth from the oil shock. Two alternative approaches, FRB/US simulations and a model estimated using exogenous oil shocks, deliver similar estimates on average.1 1 We use the series of exogenous oil shocks from Känzig (2021), “The Macroeconomic Effects of Oil Supply News: Evidence from OPEC Announcements” to estimate the effects of the current oil shock on GDP growth. Such arguments are understandable to a degree given that a fundamental identity points to a deterioration in the terms of trade being negative for real wages. More specifically, the real wage can be defined as follows where W denotes the nominal wage, Pc is the consumer price level, Py is the price level for the economy as a whole (GDP deflator), Y is real GDP and L is the level of labour inputs. W/Pc＝Y/L×WL/PyY×Py/Pc The left-hand side is the real wage obtained by dividing the nominal wage by the consumer price level. The first term on the right-hand side is productivity, the second is labour's share of income, and the third is the ratio of the economy's output price level (GDP deflator) to the consumer price level and might thus be considered the broadly defined terms of trade. It might thus appear as though the real wage (ω) is determined by productivity (a), labour's income share (λ) and the broadly defined terms of trade (θ), which may have led many to conclude that a deterioration in Japan's broadly defined terms of trade (θ) has prevented the real wage (ω) from rising even as productivity (a) has improved. An identity, not a causal relationship: It is, however, important to recognise that the above equation must be treated as a definitional accounting identity rather than as a statement of cause and effect. records.text: Aluminium – Tight inventories and better macro offset supply growth ahead Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg, SMM, Wood Mackenzie ■ In our base case (50% probability), aluminium prices remain broadly supported around $3,300 as improving macro conditions offset accelerating ex-China supply growth. The earlier reopening of the SoH helps support global activity, while lower oil prices ease inflationary pressures, contributing to a more dovish Fed, lower US real rates and a weaker dollar. These factors should help stabilise industrial demand and improve sentiment across trade-exposed sectors. However, supply growth led by Indonesia and the Middle East gradually loosens the market balance, preventing a more sustained rally despite continued inventory drawdowns and a still-tight physical market. ■ In our bull scenario (30% probability), prices rise toward $3,600/t as physical tightness persists for longer than expected while macro conditions improve. Supply growth disappoints expectations, particularly if Indonesian supply additions face commissioning delays, ramp-up challenges or slower-than-expected utilisation gains, preventing expected supply growth from materialising in full. At the same time, stronger global industrial activity, aided by a weaker dollar and improving trade flows, supports aluminium demand. records.text: Bearish coffee with 12M price outlook at $2.25/lb Source: ICO, TRS, USDA, Industry Reports, Citi Research Coffee prices have trended lower over the past month as Brazilian exports have remained exceptionally strong and inventories have begun to rebuild. Anecdotally warehouse capacity in Brazil is becoming increasingly constrained, with some facilities rejecting deliveries as stocks accumulate. We expect inventory growth to continue in the coming months as export volumes intensify, helping to alleviate the supply tightness that has supported prices in recent years. Accordingly, we maintain our bearish medium-term outlook for Arabica coffee and revise our price forecasts lower. We now expect Arabica prices at $2.50/lb over the next three months, as our previous target has already been reached, and $2.25/lb over the next 12 months. We continue to expect downside pressure on prices as larger Brazilian exports rebuild depleted global inventories, improve availability, and gradually reduce concerns about near-term supply shortages. records.text: Copper - We see flat mine supply in 2026 before return to trend Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg, Wood Mackenzie, ICSG, BGRIMM, Company Reports We see flat mine supply in 2026 (-0.2%) and overall, around-trend growth through to 2030. While higher copper prices provide an economic incentive to scale output, we apply a higher disruption allowance to account for execution risks and policy risks around medium-term supply growth. Pre-disruption, we assume a full Grasberg restart by 2028, a late-2027 Cobre Panama restart, and resilient growth from DR Congo. Ramp-ups of previously disrupted mines should boost mine output through 4Q’26 and 2027 but are subject to elevated risks of disruption and delays. We run a higher disruption allowance to account for greater uncertainty around major mine ramp- ups and DR Congo output growth resilience through 2027/2028 Copper mine supply is relying on growth from Africa (mainly DR Congo) to continue to offset development hurdles and disruptions elsewhere, e.g. Chile We expect negligible mine supply growth in 2026 and around-trend growth in 2027 and 2028 117 Prepared for Cayla Buettner

That would put us closer to the ECB’s adverse scenario, and raise risks of a fourth hike (not more), but with weaker growth, we think. Consequently, we still expect a cutting cycle to start in 2027, but perhaps at a swifter pace than we currently assume. Related to that, there are other non-linearities that are key for an ECB October move and, hence, why we don’t see it happening. For an October move we would need to see a sense of urgency and/or that the central bank feels too far from the endpoint (the desired terminal rate of the hiking cycle). Going back to ECB President Christine Lagarde’s speech at the Watchers conference, the ECB would need to perceive that we are now in the scenario that requires a forceful adjustment. Recent ECB speak, including from Lagarde herself, suggests we are still in the measured adjustment scenario. Can we move there before the October meeting? records.text: Food inflation risks rising as agricultural prices would likely further increase Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg Agricultural commodities are up ~20% year-to-date (BCOM), with significant implications for global food inflation over the coming quarters (please see the chart below). We remain bullish agricultural commodities because the market is facing an unprecedented potential shock to supply, which could result in convex price moves in a number of agricultural commodity markets, and as such the risks are skewed to the upside. The combination of bad weather, lack of crop yield maximization through reduced use of increasing expensive fertilizers, and increased vulnerability to disease (owing to the likely underuse of expensive oil-based pesticides and fungicides), could see extreme supply surprises to the downside, and convex price outcomes to the upside over the coming months. Please see slides 163-198 for details. What matters here is that, despite accelerating CPI, both the non-energy categories and input prices appear to be responding far less. That is to say we do not yet see evidence of broad-based price pressure in the economy that is likely moderating how firms experience input price inflation relative to households (see: UK Economics - UK CPI: a quiet August). For central banks, this becomes a matter of judgement. In a scenario where household expectations have diverged from firm expectations, how should the policy rate respond? This in turn is a question of the risk profile around the outlook for inflation, and whether or not the sustained pressure on energy (which households appear to be responding to) materializes in non-core inflation. A more dovish approach would be to cautiously lean on the DMP as evidence that firms are not yet planning significant price pass through. A hawkish approach would note the role of household expectation in driving pricing and wage bargaining, as well as incorporating the asymmetric and upside risk to inflation to urge a tighter policy rate. EUR HICP forecasts We expect euro-area headline HICP inflation to rise by ~50bp in September , reaching 3.75% year-on-year, its highest rate since September 2023. This would be above the Bloomberg consensus average of 3.62% (median 3.7%). We forecast HICP ex -tobacco at 3.72% ( 3.70% unrevised) , marginally below market pricing. Energy is the main driver of the expected increase, with both core and food inflation also forecast to rise. Higher petrol and diesel prices should be the main driver s, while further increases in natural gas prices are also likely to have pushed up household energy tariffs (Figure 1). records.text: The physical gold market is too small to handle wealth shifts into gold Source: Citi Research, Credit Suisse, Bloomberg The table below illustrates that the physical gold market is too small to handle wealth shifts into gold which has been true for decades. At present, the value of gold supply is around ~0.1% of total household wealth (properties, equities, bonds, cash, including that managed on their behalf by institutions, etc.) This means that a 0.1% increase, or 1/1000 th shift of household wealth into gold would require a doubling in gold mine supply. An increase from global average levels of ~3.4% to 5% would require ~18 years of mine supply. Clearly, wealth shifts cannot be accommodated, and prices need to do the work to increase the allocation to gold, by encouraging existing stockholders to rebalance their portfolio to new buyers. records.text: Aluminium – A surplus emerges, but market buffers remain thin Source: Citi Research, Wood Mackenzie, SMM, Bloomberg ■ We continue to model a primary aluminium market deficit in 2026, reflecting major supply disruptions in the Middle East and closures in Africa that offset production growth from Asian countries, notably Indonesia and Chinese production creep. As a result, primary aluminium supply growth remains significantly slower than it would otherwise have been. ■ In our base case, we expect softer semis demand growth in 2026, as energy-transition-related end-use sectors, particularly in China, expand more slowly than previously anticipated. We expect recycled metal consumption to grow more strongly than primary metal supply, albeit with a lag, absorbing part of the metal required to support semis consumption growth. Consequently, growth in primary aluminium demand remains more moderate than growth in semis demand. records.text: y that linkage materialising increases. We see the recent political noise as a timing risk for the next UK -EU summit, rather than a thesis break. The two carbon schemes are becoming increasingly compatible, and the preparatory work continues to point toward linkage as the destination (see European power and carbon update: Back to fundamentals, dated 9 September). The UK’s scheduled removal of the Carbon Price Support in April 2028 will eliminate a key asymmetry between carbon pricing in the UK and EU power sectors. Both systems have also moved toward broader maritime coverage. The ongoing UK consultation on free allocation rules for hydrogen production is explicitly designed to align with the revised EU methodology. Meanwhile, the UK's August decision to postpone waste-incineration inclusion beyond the originally planned 2028 start date could provide another avenue for convergence. The European Commission's July proposal would phase municipal waste incineration into the EU ETS from 2031 to 2034; while the UK has not yet announced a replacement start date, we think a 2031 start would offer a natural route toward greater alignment. Therefore, even in the scenario of a delayed UK -EU summit, we would expect progress updates on linkage in early 2027 to support UKA prices and narrow the EUA-UKA spread. Our previous bullish lithium call has not played out, despite tight physical market conditions, as macro headwinds and demand concerns have outweighed supportive fundamentals. Market attention has shifted to 2027, with fears of a higher battery consumption tax, potential removal of export rebates, and softer EV demand growth weighing on battery production expectations and lithium prices. A seasonal recovery in battery production in Oct/Nov’26 should support prices, however, upside is likely to be capped by producer hedging and cautious downstream restocking. ■ We are also lowering our 6-12 month price target for lithium carbonate/hydroxide/spodumene SC6 to $18k/t, $16k/t, and $1.8k/t (previously $20k/t, $18k/t and $2.2k/t), reflecting reduced conviction in the 2027 outlook. The morning panel brought together a wide array of market participants to discuss the recent TBAC charge, which investigated whether Treasury should invest some of its excess cash beyond and above the buffer it holds in the repo market. We discussed this charge in depth here, and will not rehash all those points. The panel members largely agreed that this idea has merit, but is only truly scalable in an environment in which TGCR trades above IORB, closer to a scarce reserve regime. Such arguments are understandable to a degree given that a fundamental identity points to a deterioration in the terms of trade being negative for real wages. More specifically, the real wage can be defined as follows where W denotes the nominal wage, Pc is the consumer price level, Py is the price level for the economy as a whole (GDP deflator), Y is real GDP and L is the level of labour inputs. W/Pc＝Y/L×WL/PyY×Py/Pc The left-hand side is the real wage obtained by dividing the nominal wage by the consumer price level. The first term on the right-hand side is productivity, the second is labour's share of income, and the third is the ratio of the economy's output price level (GDP deflator) to the consumer price level and might thus be considered the broadly defined terms of trade. It might thus appear as though the real wage (ω) is determined by productivity (a), labour's income share (λ) and the broadly defined terms of trade (θ), which may have led many to conclude that a deterioration in Japan's broadly defined terms of trade (θ) has prevented the real wage (ω) from rising even as productivity (a) has improved. An identity, not a causal relationship: It is, however, important to recognise that the above equation must be treated as a definitional accounting identity rather than as a statement of cause and effect. records.text: Coking Coal – Prolonged China tightness a major upside risk Source: Citi Research, Wood Mackenzie, Bloomberg ■ Global seaborne coking coal demand remains uneven, with weak Indian procurement contrasting with firm Chinese import demand. Indian buying has been weighed down by weak margins, FX headwinds and anti-dumping duties on coke imports, despite expectations for stronger steel demand post-monsoon. In China, mine safety inspections following the Shanxi accident have constrained domestic supply, while diesel shortages have raised concerns around Mongolian imports, pushing domestic prices above seaborne levels driving import demand. Although we expect domestic supply tightness to persist in the near term, a recovery in Chinese production next year could help alleviate market tightness. ■ Global supply should improve sequentially into next year although weather-related disruptions pose a downside risk into early next year. In Australia, output is expected to improve, with Centurion and Moranbah North gradually ramping up despite a weak start to the year. Canadian supply is likely to remain steady, with Elk Valley’s full-year guidance implying a stronger H2 profile. In China, domestic coal supply is likely to gradually improve into next year reducing pressure on seaborne coking coal balances. Seaborne Coking Coal S&D Balances 161 Prepared for Cayla Buettner

records.text: The global copper market has relied on rising scrap supply in 2026 to meet structural demand growth given flat mine output. However, scrap price elasticity has been much weaker than the historical relationship, which is logical given elevated energy and fuel costs, softer goods trade-in-support in China relative to last year and domestic policy headwinds including a crackdown on provincial subsidies for secondary producers and circular scrap invoicing. The global scrap supply chain is also likely relatively depleted given broader shortages of raw copper inputs for smelters in recent years and strong scrap growth in 2025. China scrap import data shows ~6% y/y growth for Jan- Aug and ICSG data suggests ~6% y/y growth in secondary refined output in 1H’26. This compares with ~12% y/y growth that might be anticipated given copper prices are ~40% higher year-on-year. China scrap imports provide a very broad measure of global copper scrap supply response China scrap imports up ~6% y/y Jan-Aug. PADD 1 inventories remain roughly 12-m bbl below seasonal norms, but could likely absorb only ~300-kb/d of additional diesel, leaving roughly 900-kb/d stranded in PADD 3 under a full export ban. records.text: An energy shock related sell-off should be temporary Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg That said, in the scenario of extreme reescalation (e.g. energy infrastructure destroyed) with much higher oil prices for longer, market focus will eventually shift from inflation to stagflation, benefiting gold in a potential replay of the prior energy crises While the negative correlation between gold and oil prices have weakened from the peak of the war, a full-blown reescalation could see a replay of oil spiking and gold suffering from degrossing Gold prices saw strong negative correlation to oil prices in the first two months of the US-Iran conflict. Much lower oil prices could see the Fed shift from hiking to cutting rates (please see chart bottom right), driving up investment demand for gold and re-igniting a momentum bull market globally underpinned by multiple structurally bullish dynamics (see slide 75 for details). Further, lower oil prices would support EM buying by increasing purchasing power. We see relatively limited downside for gold prices should the war continue on, with the potential for debasement via treasury long end buying in the face of higher inflation and bond yields. Transportation services and petroleum products account for just 1.9% of PCE, and historical relationships suggest only a modest pass-through to inflation. Fast and furious Diesel prices have recently reached new record highs and are up more than 65% since February on a monthly average basis. The increase is not solely a result of the conflict in Iran, but also reflects disruptions to refining capacity in Russia. Comparable increases have occurred only twice before in data going back to 1994: in 2008 and 2022. The surge has prompted a spate of headlines warning about potential inflationary consequences and has even led the US government to consider restrictions on diesel exports. records.text: A stronger El Niño raises operational and export risks in Brazil Source; Citi Research, Bloomberg ■ Sugarcane crushing reached 51.95 mmt, slightly above market expectations, confirming that drier weather conditions during late August supported a meaningful recovery in harvest and mill activity. While cane quality remained below last year's levels, with ATR still down roughly 4% year-over-year, the improvement in field conditions allowed mills to process more cane than anticipated. ■ More importantly, the sugar mix remained resilient at 51.8%, exceeding the 1H August level. This demonstrates that mills continued to prioritize sugar production despite lower sucrose concentration and operational challenges. The outlook remains highly dependent on September and October weather conditions. ■ Excessive rainfall during September and October could significantly disrupt harvesting and milling operations, reducing the amount of sugarcane available for processing during the most important phase of Brazil's export season. Even if total cane production ultimately remains unchanged, prolonged wet conditions can slow harvesting, lower crushing rates, increase field losses, and delay sugar shipments to global markets. 186 Prepared for Cayla Buettner

records.text: Coking Coal – China domestic tightness to support seaborne prices Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg Australia PHCC FOB coking coal price scenarios China’s coking coal output impacted by mine safety inspections ■ Base Case (60% probability) – We remain neutral on coking coal and expect prices to stay elevated in the near term amid persistent tightness in Chinese domestic supply. We maintain our 0-3 month price target of $250/t for Australian FOB PLV coking coal. Chinese supply constraints, driven by heightened mine safety inspections following recent accidents, concerns over Mongolian export availability, and weather-related disruptions to Indonesian coke supply, have underpinned a ~US$70/t rally in seaborne prices since early August. Much of the strength appears to have been driven by precautionary buying from Chinese traders and end-users ahead of the holiday season. However, we believe risks are becoming more balanced. Weak steel mill margins, uncertainty around Chinese steel production and subdued Indian buying interest at current price levels continue to weigh on sentiment. While a meaningful recovery in Chinese domestic coking coal output has yet to materialize, ongoing diesel shortages may further constrain Mongolian supply. In addition, seasonal wet weather in Australia from November could disrupt exports and provide further support to prices. records.text: r to manage and moderate policy goals. It would also translate to more Democratic wins at the Gubernatorial and state legislature level too. That could potentially hasten passage of the AI/data center regulation, though this is not only a Democratic issue at this point. The primary downside risk in this scenario is a risk-off market reaction driven by concerns about increased regulation, particularly policies perceived as threatening the data center investment cycle. Even so, the absence of a veto-proof Senate majority makes significant legislative action unlikely in our view. As a result, any initial market selloff could fade as investors reassess the practical constraints on policymaking. Republican sweep: more defense spend, higher deficits A Republican sweep could prove somewhat more supportive of growth than either a divided Congress or a Democratic sweep. The primary reason is our expectation that Republicans would use reconciliation to enact a larger increase in defense spending for FY2027. Assuming defense spending rises by roughly $150 billion above our baseline, we estimate that it would add approximately 0.1 percentage points to GDP growth in FY2027 and 0.2 percentage points in FY2028. Some of these gains, however, could be offset by reductions in non-defense spending and higher interest rates stemming from larger fiscal deficits. Beyond defense spending, a Republican sweep helps the administration’s deregulatory agenda and is unlikely to trigger a sell-off in risk

records.text: 28 September 2026 Fixed Income Blog Page 8 Deutsche Securities Inc. In London we were invariably asked what would change if anything did. Our answer is that two smaller changes are far more plausible than moving the 25% target. The first is a wider deviation band. Restoring the domestic bond band from plus or minus 6% to the 7% of the fourth period, or widening it further, leaves the expected return and risk assumptions behind the 25% target untouched and sits within the flexibility the medium-term plan already grants for tactical positioning based on a reasoned market outlook. Each percentage point of band is worth about JPY3.2trn on assets of JPY317.8trn, and government officials are reported to regard flexibility within the existing ranges as the more practical option than a change to the Basic Portfolio. The second is a longer duration within the domestic bond allocation. GPIF's domestic bonds are managed against NOMURA-BPI (excluding ABS) as the policy benchmark, whose duration was 7.6 years at end-August (average maturity 10.2 years), almost a year shorter than the 8.5 years of March 2025 as higher yields and the Ministry of Finance's super-long cuts have worked through the index. Highlights this week There is a lot of central bank speak this week, including 18 appearances by Fed officials, in which we hopefully get more clarity on the Fed’s reaction function (see our US weekly for a discussion of how hikes are likely to exacerbate existing imbalances). records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 and impaired Hormuz traffic tighten effective capacity across several routes simultaneously. The system remains far from the extremes of 2021-22, but supply- chain normalization had been an important source of goods disinflation, and that tailwind is fading. Hormuz also reaches beyond energy because lower bulk and container traffic can restrict fertilizers, petrochemicals, aluminum, and other industrial intermediates. The risk is not one isolated bottleneck, but several upstream pressures are becoming harder to absorb at the same time. The bottom line is that non-core shocks become macro-relevant when persistence outlasts the buffers that initially contain them. Energy delivers the fastest and largest impulse; food is slower but more durable; and logistics and other upstream constraints can reinforce both. We still expect disinflation to continue, but the process is becoming less linear. For central banks, the relevant question is increasingly not whether headline inflation rises but whether persistent upstream pressure survives long enough to enter core prices, expectations, and wages. We still expect disinflation to continue, but the margin for error is narrowing as the global economy may have to absorb several supply shocks at once.

records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures 28 September 2026 3 So why is Japan worse off? The answer is that Japanese firms have taken a very different approach to pricing than their German and French counterparts, opting not to hike export prices even when import costs are rising and focusing instead on limiting wage expenses to remain profitable. Unit labour costs have effectively been kept under control by restricting increases in nominal wages even when productivity has improved, thereby enabling firms to stay in the black without needing to offset higher import costs by raising export prices. It should thus be clear that a deterioration in Japan's narrowly defined terms of trade is not simply an exogenous phenomenon attributable solely to higher import prices. Much of the time, it has been due to firms limiting their wage outlays to keep selling their products cheaply even when import costs have been rising. To put this another way, while the terms of trade might at first glance appear to be a neutral indicator of relative prices, they are actually liable to be heavily influenced by the behaviour of Japanese firms if wage suppression is used as the primary strategy for maintaining price competitiveness and profitability. In summary, both broadly and narrowly defined terms of trade have deteriorated due to a combination of exogenous import price shocks and corporate strategies that prioritise profit margins over productivity-linked
